docs.title: Chapter 6: An Outline of Sanskrit Grammar: Sandhi, Compounds, Case and Verb
docs.text:
arthapravṛttitattvānāṃ śabdā eva nibandhanam tattvāvabodhaḥ śabdānāṃ nāsti vyākaraṇād ṛte Words alone are the means by which the truth about things and their uses is fixed; and without grammar there is no true understanding of words.

— Bhartṛhari, Vākyapadīya 1.13

docs.title: 6.1 Introduction
docs.text: Chapter 5 described the Aṣṭādhyāyī as a system of rules. This chapter is its companion: a reference outline of the Sanskrit that those rules describe, for readers who want to see the language itself before following the grammarians’ debates in the chapters that come next. It covers the combination of sounds (sandhi), the formation of compounds (samāsa), the case system, the derivation of words by suffixes, and the verb. Pāṇini’s rule numbers are given where they help to show how the traditional grammar treats each topic. For fuller modern accounts, see the standard reference grammars and Cardona (1997); for the Pāṇinian treatment of individual rules, Katre (1987) and Sharma (1987–2003).

docs.title: 6.2 Sandhi
docs.text: Sandhi (“joining”) is the set of sound changes that take place where elements meet: within a word, between the members of a compound, and between words in a sentence. In written Sanskrit external sandhi is normally applied, so that a sentence may appear as one continuous string. This is one reason why reading Sanskrit, and processing it by computer (Chapter 14), requires a sound knowledge of sandhi.

docs.title: 6.2.1 Vowel sandhi
docs.text:
The principal rules are set out in Table 6.1; Figure 6.1 arranges them as a sequence of decisions.

Table 6.1. Principal rules of vowel sandhi Meeting vowels Result Rule and example similar vowels (a/ā + a/ā, i/ī + i/ī …) long vowel 6.1.101; deva + ālaya \(\rightarrow\) devālaya a/ā + i/ī e 6.1.87 (guṇa); deva + indra \(\rightarrow\) devendra a/ā + u/ū o 6.1.87; sūrya + udaya \(\rightarrow\) sūryodaya a/ā + ṛ ar 6.1.87; mahā + ṛṣi \(\rightarrow\) maharṣi a/ā + e/ai ai 6.1.88 (vṛddhi); sadā + eva \(\rightarrow\) sadaiva a/ā + o/au au 6.1.88; mahā + oṣadhi \(\rightarrow\) mahauṣadhi i/ī, u/ū, ṛ + dissimilar vowel y, v, r + vowel 6.1.77; iti + ādi \(\rightarrow\) ityādi word-final e, o + a e, o; a elided 6.1.109; vane + atra \(\rightarrow\) vane ’tra Figure 6.1. Simplified decision chart for the main rules of vowel sandhi

docs.title: 6.2.2 Consonant sandhi
docs.text:
Table 6.2 gives some of the commonest rules for consonants.

Table 6.2. Some rules of consonant sandhi Process Description Example Voicing A word-final stop becomes voiced before a voiced sound vāk + devī \(\rightarrow\) vāgdevī Palatal assimilation Final t becomes c or j before palatals tat + ca \(\rightarrow\) tac ca; tat + jayati \(\rightarrow\) taj jayati Nasal assimilation A final stop may become the nasal of its class before a nasal tat + na \(\rightarrow\) tan na; jagat + nātha \(\rightarrow\) jagannātha Sibilant after a stop After a stop, initial ś may become ch tat + śrutvā \(\rightarrow\) tac chrutvā Anusvāra Final m becomes anusvāra before a consonant tam + karoti \(\rightarrow\) taṃ karoti Retroflexion of n n becomes ṇ after r, ṛ, ṣ within a word, if nothing but vowels, gutturals, labials, h, y, v or anusvāra intervene rāmeṇa, karaṇa (8.4.1–2) Retroflexion of s s becomes ṣ after i, u, ṛ, e, o, k, r agni + su \(\rightarrow\) agniṣu (8.3.59)

docs.title: 6.2.3 Sandhi of visarga
docs.text:
The visarga (-ḥ) changes according to the sound that follows (Table 6.3).

Table 6.3. Main rules for final -ḥ (visarga) Before Change Example c, ch ḥ \(\rightarrow\) ś rāmaḥ + ca \(\rightarrow\) rāmaś ca ṭ, ṭh ḥ \(\rightarrow\) ṣ rāmaḥ + ṭīkām \(\rightarrow\) rāmaṣ ṭīkām t, th ḥ \(\rightarrow\) s rāmaḥ + tatra \(\rightarrow\) rāmas tatra k, kh, p, ph, sibilants ḥ remains rāmaḥ karoti voiced consonant (after a) -aḥ \(\rightarrow\) -o rāmaḥ + gacchati \(\rightarrow\) rāmo gacchati a (after a) -aḥ \(\rightarrow\) -o, a elided rāmaḥ + atra \(\rightarrow\) rāmo ’tra other vowels (after a) -aḥ \(\rightarrow\) -a rāmaḥ + iti \(\rightarrow\) rāma iti voiced sound (after i, u etc.) ḥ \(\rightarrow\) r muniḥ + gacchati \(\rightarrow\) munir gacchati

docs.title: 6.3 Compounds (samāsa)
docs.text:
Sanskrit forms compounds very freely: two or more stems are joined, and only the last carries a case ending. Pāṇini treats compounds in Adhyāya 2.1–2.2; the tradition distinguishes four main types (Table 6.4).

Table 6.4. The four main types of compound Type Character Example avyayībhāva Adverbial; first member usually an indeclinable yathāśakti “according to one’s ability” tatpuruṣa Determinative; the last member is qualified by the first rājapuruṣa “the king’s man” dvandva Copulative; members coordinated rāmalakṣmaṇau “Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa” bahuvrīhi Possessive; the compound describes something outside itself pītāmbara “(one) whose garment is yellow”, i.e. Kṛṣṇa

The name bahuvrīhi is itself an example: “(one) who has much rice”, i.e. a wealthy man. The same two words can form compounds of different types with different meanings: nīlotpala as a tatpuruṣa (more precisely a karmadhāraya) means “blue lotus”; as a bahuvrīhi it would mean “(a pond) that has blue lotuses”. In the Vedic language the accent distinguished such pairs, as the story of indraśatru shows (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 6.3.1 Kinds of tatpuruṣa
docs.text:
Tatpuruṣa compounds are named after the case relation of the first member to the second (Table 6.5).

Table 6.5. Tatpuruṣa compounds named after the case relation of the first member, with traditional examples Relation Example accusative kṛṣṇaśrita “resorting to Kṛṣṇa” instrumental śaṅkulākhaṇḍa “cut with a knife” dative yūpadāru “wood for a sacrificial post” ablative corabhaya “fear of thieves” genitive rājapuruṣa “king’s man” locative akṣaśauṇḍa “skilled at dice” Karmadhāraya a tatpuruṣa whose members refer to the same thing: nīlotpala “blue lotus”, mahārāja “great king”. Dvigu a karmadhāraya whose first member is a numeral: triloka or trilokī “the three worlds”, pañcavaṭī “(the place of) five banyan trees”. Nañ-tatpuruṣa a compound with the negative prefix a(n)-: abrāhmaṇa “non-Brahmin”, adharma. Upapada a compound whose second member is a verbal derivative that occurs only in composition: kumbhakāra “potter”, literally “pot-maker”. Aluk a compound in which the first member keeps its case ending: parasmaipada (“word for another”), with the dative parasmai.

Pāṇini also lists irregular compounds in a group beginning with mayūravyaṃsaka (2.1.72), which are accepted as they occur in usage.

docs.title: 6.3.2 Long compounds
docs.text: Classical prose, above all the novels of Bāṇa (7th century) and Subandhu, and much technical and philosophical writing, uses compounds of great length. They must be analysed layer by layer. An illustrative example: nīlotpaladalaśyāmā is a bahuvrīhi, “(a woman) dark like the petal of a blue lotus”. Within it, nīlotpala (“blue lotus”) is a karmadhāraya; nīlotpaladala (“petal of a blue lotus”) a genitive tatpuruṣa; nīlotpaladalaśyāma (“dark as a blue lotus petal”) a compound of comparison.

docs.title: 6.4 The Case System
docs.text:
Sanskrit nouns have seven cases (vibhakti) in three numbers (singular, dual and plural). The vocative (sambodhana, “address”) is not a separate case in Pāṇini’s system but a use of the nominative (2.3.47–49); the special vocative singular form is called sambuddhi. Modern grammars usually list it as an eighth case (Tables 6.6, 6.7 and 6.8).

Table 6.6. The Sanskrit cases and their principal uses No. Name Modern term Principal uses 1 prathamā nominative The bare meaning of the stem; the agent of an active verb, the object of a passive one 2 dvitīyā accusative The object (karman); goal of motion; duration 3 tṛtīyā instrumental Instrument (karaṇa); agent of a passive verb; accompaniment 4 caturthī dative Recipient (sampradāna); purpose 5 pañcamī ablative Point of departure (apādāna); cause; comparison 6 ṣaṣṭhī genitive “Other” relations, such as possession (not a kāraka) 7 saptamī locative Locus (adhikaraṇa) in space or time; the “locative absolute” – sambodhana vocative Address; a use of the nominative Table 6.7. Declension of deva “god” (masculine stem in -a) Case Singular Dual Plural Nominative devaḥ devau devāḥ Accusative devam devau devān Instrumental devena devābhyām devaiḥ Dative devāya devābhyām devebhyaḥ Ablative devāt devābhyām devebhyaḥ Genitive devasya devayoḥ devānām Locative deve devayoḥ deveṣu Vocative deva devau devāḥ Table 6.8. Declension of latā “creeper” (feminine stem in -ā) Case Singular Dual Plural Nominative latā late latāḥ Accusative latām late latāḥ Instrumental latayā latābhyām latābhiḥ Dative latāyai latābhyām latābhyaḥ Ablative latāyāḥ latābhyām latābhyaḥ Genitive latāyāḥ latayoḥ latānām Locative latāyām latayoḥ latāsu Vocative late late latāḥ

Sanskrit has many more declension classes, distinguished by the final sound of the stem and by gender: stems in -i and -u, in -ī and -ū, in -ṛ (such as pitṛ “father” and mātṛ “mother”), and a variety of consonant stems, some of which change their form between “strong” and “weak” cases (rājā, rājānam, but rājñā, rājñaḥ). Pāṇini handles this variety with a single set of basic endings (sup) added to all stems, and a large number of rules that modify stems and endings in particular environments. Two further paradigms, a vowel stem in -i and a consonant stem in -an, are given in Table 6.9; the alternation of strong and weak stems in rājan is a feature that Sanskrit inherited from Indo-European. The kāraka system that underlies the assignment of all these cases is described in Chapter 5.

Table 6.9. Declension of agni “fire” (masculine stem in -i) and rājan “king” (masculine stem in -an) agni rājan Case Sg. Du. Pl. Sg. Du. Pl. Nom. agniḥ agnī agnayaḥ rājā rājānau rājānaḥ Acc. agnim agnī agnīn rājānam rājānau rājñaḥ Ins. agninā agnibhyām agnibhiḥ rājñā rājabhyām rājabhiḥ Dat. agnaye agnibhyām agnibhyaḥ rājñe rājabhyām rājabhyaḥ Abl. agneḥ agnibhyām agnibhyaḥ rājñaḥ rājabhyām rājabhyaḥ Gen. agneḥ agnyoḥ agnīnām rājñaḥ rājñoḥ rājñām Loc. agnau agnyoḥ agniṣu rājñi, rājani rājñoḥ rājasu Voc. agne agnī agnayaḥ rājan rājānau rājānaḥ

docs.title: 6.4.1 Pronouns
docs.text:
The pronouns have partly separate endings of their own. The demonstrative tad “that, he” has the dative, ablative and locative singular tasmai, tasmāt and tasmin, with an element -sm- that does not appear in the nouns, and the nominative plural te instead of -āḥ. (In Pali these pronominal endings spread to the nouns: Chapter 9.) The personal pronouns of the first and second persons have no gender, are built on different stems in the singular and plural, and have short unaccented forms (me, te, naḥ, vaḥ) that cannot begin a sentence (Table 6.10).

Table 6.10. Pronouns: aham “I”, tvam “you” and tad “that, he” (masculine), singular and plural Case I we you (sg.) you (pl.) he they Nom. aham vayam tvam yūyam saḥ te Acc. mām asmān tvām yuṣmān tam tān Ins. mayā asmābhiḥ tvayā yuṣmābhiḥ tena taiḥ Dat. mahyam asmabhyam tubhyam yuṣmabhyam tasmai tebhyaḥ Abl. mat asmat tvat yuṣmat tasmāt tebhyaḥ Gen. mama asmākam tava yuṣmākam tasya teṣām Loc. mayi asmāsu tvayi yuṣmāsu tasmin teṣu

docs.title: 6.5 Primary Derivatives (kṛt)
docs.text:
Suffixes added directly to roots form nouns, adjectives, participles, infinitives and absolutives. Pāṇini’s names for them include marker letters, which are shown in the second column (Table 6.11).

Table 6.11. Some primary (kṛt) suffixes Suffix Pāṇini’s name Function Example -ta kta past passive participle kṛta “done”, gata “gone” -tavat ktavatu past active participle gatavat “having gone” -at/-ant śatṛ present active participle pacat “cooking” -māna/-āna śānac present middle participle pacamāna “cooking (for oneself)” -tṛ tṛc agent noun kartṛ “doer” -aka ṇvul agent noun pācaka “cook” -ana lyuṭ action or instrument noun karaṇa “doing, instrument” -tum tumun infinitive gantum “to go” -tvā, -ya ktvā, lyap absolutive kṛtvā “having done”; prakṛtya (with a preverb) -tavya, -anīya, -ya tavyat, anīyar, ṇyat gerundives kartavya, karaṇīya, kārya “to be done”

docs.title: 6.6 Secondary Derivatives (taddhita)
docs.text:
Secondary suffixes are added to nominal stems. Pāṇini treats them in Adhyāyas 4 and 5 (Table 6.12).

Table 6.12. Some secondary (taddhita) suffixes Meaning Suffix Example Patronymic -i (iñ), -a with vṛddhi (aṇ), -ya (yañ) dāśarathi “son of Daśaratha”; vāsudeva “son of Vasudeva”; gārgya “descendant of Garga” Relation -ika (ṭhak etc.), -īya (cha) vaidika “Vedic”, dhārmika “righteous”, pāṇinīya “Pāṇinian” Abstract nouns -tva, -tā manuṣyatva “humanity”, sundaratā “beauty” Possession -mat/-vat, -in dhanavat “wealthy”, yogin Material -maya suvarṇamaya “golden” Time -ika dainika “daily”, māsika “monthly” Place adverbs -tra, -tas tatra “there”, yatra “where”, tatas “from there” Diminutive -ka putraka “little son”

Primary and secondary derivation, together with compounding, make the Sanskrit vocabulary highly productive and transparent: from the root kṛ “do, make” come kartṛ “doer”, karaṇa “instrument”, karman “action”, kārya “what is to be done”, kṛti “a work”, and with preverbs prakṛti “nature, base”, vikṛti “modification”, saṃskāra “refinement”, ākṛti “form”. This productivity is why Sanskrit has been a source of technical vocabulary for many Indian languages, including the coinages of modern Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Telugu and Kannada.

docs.title: 6.7.1 Tenses and moods (lakāra)
docs.text:
Pāṇini designates the tenses and moods by ten abstract elements, all beginning with l (hence lakāra), which are later replaced by the personal endings. The optative liṅ has two forms, the ordinary optative and the benedictive (Tables 6.13 and 6.14).

Table 6.13. The ten lakāras, illustrated with the root bhū “be, become” (3rd person singular active) Lakāra Modern term Pāṇini’s characterisation Form laṭ present present time (3.2.123) bhavati liṭ perfect past, not witnessed by the speaker (parokṣa) babhūva luṭ periphrastic future future, not of today bhavitā lṛṭ simple future future bhaviṣyati leṭ subjunctive Vedic only bhavāti loṭ imperative command, request bhavatu laṅ imperfect past, not of today abhavat liṅ (vidhi) optative injunction, possibility bhavet liṅ (āśīḥ) benedictive blessing bhūyāt luṅ aorist past in general abhūt lṛṅ conditional unrealised condition abhaviṣyat Table 6.14. Present tense (laṭ) of bhū (active) and edh “prosper” (middle) Active (parasmaipada) Middle (ātmanepada) Person Sg. Du. Pl. Sg. Du. Pl. 3rd bhavati bhavataḥ bhavanti edhate edhete edhante 2nd bhavasi bhavathaḥ bhavatha edhase edhethe edhadhve 1st bhavāmi bhavāvaḥ bhavāmaḥ edhe edhāvahe edhāmahe

The Indian grammarians list the persons in the order third, second, first (prathama, madhyama, uttama puruṣa), as in the table; European grammars reverse the order. Table 6.15 gives the other common active forms of the same root.

Table 6.15. Other tenses and moods of bhū (active) Imperfect (laṅ) Optative (liṅ) Imperative (loṭ) Perfect (liṭ) Future (lṛṭ) 3rd sg. abhavat bhavet bhavatu babhūva bhaviṣyati 3rd du. abhavatām bhavetām bhavatām babhūvatuḥ bhaviṣyataḥ 3rd pl. abhavan bhaveyuḥ bhavantu babhūvuḥ bhaviṣyanti 2nd sg. abhavaḥ bhaveḥ bhava babhūvitha bhaviṣyasi 2nd du. abhavatam bhavetam bhavatam babhūvathuḥ bhaviṣyathaḥ 2nd pl. abhavata bhaveta bhavata babhūva bhaviṣyatha 1st sg. abhavam bhaveyam bhavāni babhūva bhaviṣyāmi 1st du. abhavāva bhaveva bhavāva babhūviva bhaviṣyāvaḥ 1st pl. abhavāma bhavema bhavāma babhūvima bhaviṣyāmaḥ

Table 6.15 shows several characteristic devices of the Sanskrit verb: the augment a- that marks the imperfect (and the aorist and conditional) as past; the optative element -e- (historically -ai-, from -a- + -ī-); the reduplication of the root in the perfect (ba-bhūva); and the future suffix -sya-, here -iṣya-.

In classical Sanskrit the distinctions between the three past tenses were largely lost, and the past passive participle increasingly took over their functions, a development continued in the modern Indo-Aryan languages.

docs.title: 6.7.2 Active and middle (parasmaipada, ātmanepada)
docs.text: Verbs take one of two sets of endings: parasmaipada (“word for another”) and ātmanepada (“word for oneself”). Some roots take only one set, others both (ubhayapada). For roots that take both, the traditional rule is that the middle endings are used when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (yajate “he sacrifices for himself”) and the active endings otherwise (yajati “he sacrifices (for another)”), though in classical usage the distinction is often not observed. The passive is formed with the middle endings and the suffix -ya- (kriyate “is done”), introduced by rule 3.1.67 (sārvadhātuke yak).

docs.title: 6.7.3 Derivative verbs
docs.text:
Besides the simple root, Sanskrit forms several kinds of derivative verb stems, which Pāṇini introduces at the beginning of Adhyāya 3 and then treats as roots in their own right (3.1.32 sanādyantā dhātavaḥ):

Causative with the suffix ṇic (3.1.26), for an action that the subject causes another to perform: bhāvayati “causes to be”, kārayati “causes to do, has made”, pācayati “has (someone) cook”. Desiderative with the suffix san and reduplication (3.1.7), for an action that the subject wishes to perform: bubhūṣati “wishes to be”, jigamiṣati “wishes to go”, pipāsati “wishes to drink, is thirsty”. Intensive with the suffix yaṅ and a strengthened reduplication (3.1.22), for an action repeated or done intensely: bobhūyate, jaṅgamyate “goes to and fro”. Denominative formed from nouns, for example with kyac (3.1.8) in the sense of wishing for something for oneself: putrīyati “wishes for a son”.

The causative is by far the most common of these in the classical language, and the desiderative supplies many ordinary nouns and adjectives (pipāsā “thirst”, jijñāsā “desire to know, inquiry”, mumukṣu “one who desires liberation”). The last two words show how the grammatical categories entered the vocabulary of philosophy: the Brahmasūtra opens with athāto brahmajijñāsā, “now, therefore, the desire to know brahman”.

docs.title: 6.7.4 Vowel gradation
docs.text:
Many Sanskrit forms alternate between three grades of a vowel: the basic grade, guṇa and vṛddhi (Table 6.16).

Table 6.16. Vowel gradation: basic, guṇa and vṛddhi grades Basic grade guṇa vṛddhi i, ī e ai u, ū o au ṛ, ṝ ar ār ḷ al āl a a ā

Pāṇini’s first two rules define vṛddhi and guṇa (1.1.1–2). The alternations they describe are of Indo-European origin, and the terms guṇa and vṛddhi were adopted by 19th-century European comparative philologists in describing the vowel gradation (ablaut) of other Indo-European languages (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 6.8 Vedic and Classical Sanskrit
docs.text:
Pāṇini described both the Vedic language (chandas) and the spoken Sanskrit (bhāṣā) of his day, and the differences between them are considerable. The Vedic language has a richer verbal system, including a subjunctive (leṭ) and an injunctive, and a dozen or more infinitive forms (such as -tave, -dhyai, -tos), where Classical Sanskrit has only -tum. Vedic nouns show more varied endings (for example the nominative plural devāsaḥ beside devāḥ, and the instrumental plural devebhiḥ beside devaiḥ). Preverbs may stand apart from their verbs (tmesis). Above all, Vedic has a pitch accent, which Pāṇini describes in detail and which was lost in Classical Sanskrit.

The Classical language that Pāṇini’s grammar fixed was used for over two thousand years with remarkably little change in its morphology. Its vocabulary, style and syntax, however, did change: later prose favours long compounds and nominal constructions, the past passive participle displaces the finite past tenses, and many words acquire new meanings or are borrowed from the Prakrits, the Dravidian languages and Persian. The grammar’s rules ensured the stability of forms; usage continued to evolve within them.

docs.title: 6.9 A Sentence Analysed
docs.text:
The pieces described in this chapter come together in the simplest sentence. Consider:

devadattaḥ kuṭhāreṇa vṛkṣaṃ chinatti “Devadatta cuts the tree with an axe.”

  • chinatti is the third person singular active present of the root chid “cut”, a root of the seventh class, which inserts a nasal into the root to form its present stem (chi-na-t-ti). The active ending expresses the agent (kartṛ).

  • Because the agent is already expressed by the verb ending, the word for the agent, devadatta, takes only the nominative, which expresses “the bare meaning of the stem” (2.3.46).

  • vṛkṣam “tree” is the object (karman), what the agent most wishes to reach by the action (1.4.49), and takes the accusative (2.3.2).

  • kuṭhāreṇa “with an axe” is the instrument (karaṇa), the most effective means (1.4.42), and takes the instrumental (2.3.18); its ṇ results from the retroflexion rule after r.

  • Final -m before a consonant becomes anusvāra: vṛkṣaṃ chinatti.

In the passive the same participants are presented differently: devadattena kuṭhāreṇa vṛkṣaś chidyate “the tree is cut by Devadatta with an axe”. Now the verb (chid + passive -ya- + middle ending) expresses the object, so vṛkṣa stands in the nominative and the agent devadatta in the instrumental; the visarga of vṛkṣaḥ becomes ś before ch. Because case endings, not position, mark the relations, the words of either sentence may be rearranged for emphasis or metre without changing who does what to whom. This is the sense in which Sanskrit word order is “free”, though prose has a normal order (agent, object, verb) and departures from it are marked.

docs.title: 6.10 The Architecture of the System
docs.text:
Figure 6.2 brings together the stages by which the Pāṇinian system builds words and sentences.

Figure 6.2. A simplified picture of word and sentence formation in the Pāṇinian system

The kāraka analysis used in this chapter has also been applied directly in the computational analysis of Sanskrit and Hindi, notably in the “Paninian Grammar Framework” of Akshar Bharati, Vineet Chaitanya and Rajeev Sangal (Bharati et al. 1995); its modern comparisons and limits are discussed in Section 5.7 and Chapter 14.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Kātyāyana and Patañjali: The Mahābhāṣya
docs.text:
atha śabdānuśāsanam Now [begins] the instruction in words.

— opening words of Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya

docs.title: 7.1 The Three Sages
docs.text:
The later tradition regarded three authors as the founding authorities of Sanskrit grammar, the “three sages” (munitraya): Pāṇini (c. 4th century BCE) for the rules (sūtra); Kātyāyana (c. 3rd century BCE) for the critical notes on them (vārttika); and Patañjali (mid-2nd century BCE) for the great commentary (bhāṣya) that discusses both. “The grammar of the three sages” (trimuni vyākaraṇam) became a common name for the Pāṇinian system, and a maxim of the tradition holds that where the three differ, the later carries greater authority (yathottaraṃ munīnāṃ prāmāṇyam). In practice this meant that Patañjali’s judgements, where he decides that a rule is unnecessary or should be read differently, were accepted by later grammarians (Figure 7.1).

Figure 7.1. The three sages of Pāṇinian grammar and their works

docs.title: 7.2 Kātyāyana’s Vārttikas
docs.text:
A vārttika, according to a definition current in the later tradition, is a work that considers what has been said, what has not been said and what has been badly said (ukta, anukta, durukta) in a basic text. Kātyāyana’s notes do exactly this. They test Pāṇini’s rules against usage, point out cases where a rule is too wide or too narrow, propose additional rules, and sometimes argue that a rule is unnecessary. They survive only as embedded in Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya; Franz Kielhorn showed in 1876 how they can be separated from Patañjali’s own prose (Kielhorn 1876). Kātyāyana is traditionally identified with the author of the Vājasaneyi Prātiśākhya (Chapter 2), but the identification is uncertain.

Some of Kātyāyana’s notes record forms that Pāṇini’s rules do not produce, and scholars have long debated whether they show changes in the language between the two authors, regional differences, or simply oversights by Pāṇini (Cardona 1976; Deshpande 1993).

The first of Kātyāyana’s notes, discussed at length by Patañjali, states the presuppositions of the whole enterprise:

Kātyāyana, first vārttika

siddhe śabdārthasambandhe lokato ’rthaprayukte śabdaprayoge śāstreṇa dharmaniyamaḥ

“Since word, meaning and the relation between them are established, and since, following everyday usage, words are used in order to convey meanings, the science [of grammar] lays down a restriction for the sake of merit (dharma).”

The grammarian, in other words, does not create words or their meanings: these are given by usage. What grammar adds is a restriction (niyama) that distinguishes correct forms, whose use brings religious merit, from incorrect ones. Patañjali took siddha (“established”) to mean “eternal” (nitya), and the line became the starting point for long discussions of whether words are eternal.

docs.title: 7.3.1 Date
docs.text: Patañjali’s date is one of the better-fixed points in early Indian chronology. In discussing the use of the present tense for an action still in progress he gives the example (on rule 3.2.123) iha puṣyamitraṃ yājayāmaḥ (“here we are performing sacrifices for Puṣyamitra”), referring to the founder of the Śuṅga dynasty, who ruled from about 185 BCE. To illustrate the imperfect tense for a recent event that the speaker could have witnessed, he gives (on 3.2.111) aruṇad yavanaḥ sāketam (“the Yavana besieged Sāketa”) and aruṇad yavano madhyamikām (“the Yavana besieged Madhyamikā”), usually taken to refer to an Indo-Greek incursion into the Gangetic plain in the 2nd century BCE. Patañjali is therefore generally dated to the mid-2nd century BCE (Cardona 1976; Scharfe 1977).

docs.title: 7.3.2 Identity
docs.text:
A later tradition identifies the grammarian Patañjali with the author of the Yogasūtra and with a writer on medicine. It is expressed in a verse, of uncertain and probably medieval origin, often recited before study:

Traditional verse (late; source uncertain)

yogena cittasya padena vācāṃ malaṃ śarīrasya ca vaidyakena yo ’pākarot taṃ pravaraṃ munīnāṃ patañjaliṃ prāñjalir ānato ’smi

“With joined palms I bow to Patañjali, foremost of sages, who removed the impurity of the mind by yoga, of speech by grammar, and of the body by medicine.”

Most modern scholars distinguish the grammarian from the author of the Yogasūtra, which is now generally dated to c. 325–425 CE; the two works differ in vocabulary, style and doctrine.

docs.title: 7.4 Structure of the Mahābhāṣya
docs.text:
The Mahābhāṣya is divided into eighty-five “daily lessons” (āhnika), following the order of Pāṇini’s rules. It does not comment on every rule: it takes up rather less than half of them, mostly those on which Kātyāyana has notes, and sometimes others. Its method is that of dialogue. An objector raises a difficulty; another voice replies; the discussion moves through several rounds, often ending with Patañjali’s decision (siddhānta). The style is conversational, full of homely examples and illustrations from daily life, and it is one of the finest pieces of early Sanskrit prose (Joshi and Roodbergen 1986). See Figure 7.2.

Figure 7.2. The pattern of argument in the Mahābhāṣya

docs.title: 7.5 The Introductory Lesson (Paspaśāhnika)
docs.text: The first lesson, known as the Paspaśāhnika (“introduction”), is the most widely read part of the work. Here Patañjali asks what grammar is, why it should be studied, and what a word is (Joshi and Roodbergen 1986).

docs.title: 7.5.1 Why study grammar?
docs.text:
Patañjali gives five principal purposes, summed up in the compound rakṣo­hāgama­laghv­asandehāḥ prayojanam (Table 7.1).

Table 7.1. The five principal purposes of grammar in the Paspaśāhnika Purpose Explanation rakṣā (protection) Grammar protects the Vedas: one who knows it can tell where sounds have been lost, added or altered ūha (adaptation) Ritual formulas must be adapted to new contexts (for example by changing gender or number), which requires knowledge of grammar āgama (scriptural injunction) A Vedic statement prescribes that a Brahmin should study the Veda with its six auxiliaries, of which grammar is the chief laghu (economy) Grammar is the shortest route to the knowledge of words asandeha (removal of doubt) Grammar resolves ambiguities, for example by showing which compound type, and so which meaning, an accent pattern indicates

To illustrate economy, Patañjali tells how Bṛhaspati taught Indra the words of the language one by one, for a thousand divine years, without reaching the end. Since nobody can learn an infinite list, words must be learned through general rules with exceptions. He then lists further purposes, each tied to a Vedic text. One recalls the story, from the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, of the Asuras who were defeated because they mispronounced a ritual cry, and draws the moral that a Brahmin must not speak “barbarously” (na mlecchitavai), for an incorrect word is a mleccha. Another cites the verse, also found in the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā, about the sacrificer whose wrongly accented word indraśatru turned against him (Chapter 2). Another gives a grammatical reading of the Vedic riddle verse about the “four horns” of speech (Ṛgveda 4.58.3).

Patañjali is also clear that grammar does not create language. In a famous comparison, he observes that someone who needs a pot goes to the potter’s house and says “make me a pot, I have work to do with it”; but nobody who wants to use words goes to a grammarian’s house and asks him to make words. Words are taken from the world of usage, and grammar only regulates their correct use. This priority of usage over rule, already stated in Kātyāyana’s first note, is one of the foundations of the Pāṇinian tradition.

docs.title: 7.5.2 What is a word?
docs.text:
Patañjali begins with a famous question: in the utterance gauḥ (“cow”), what is the word? It is not the animal with its dewlap, tail, hump, hooves and horns; that is the thing meant (dravya). It is not the action, the quality or the universal. “That by whose utterance there arises the understanding of [a thing with] dewlap, tail, hump, hooves and horns, that is the word.” Or, as he also puts it, in common usage a sound by which a meaning is understood is called a word.

He also discusses whether the word is eternal (nitya) or produced (kārya). He notes that the question had been examined in detail in the Saṃgraha, a lost work attributed to Vyāḍi, and concludes that on either view grammar is to be undertaken. Elsewhere (on rule 1.1.70) he distinguishes the word itself, the sphoṭa, from the audible sound (dhvani) that is its quality: the same word may be uttered quickly or slowly, by different voices, just as a drum struck once may be heard far or near. This brief remark became the seed of Bhartṛhari’s much larger theory (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 7.5.3 Universal or individual?
docs.text: Does a word denote a universal (ākṛti, “form”) or an individual thing (dravya)? Kātyāyana reports two earlier grammarians who held opposite views: Vājapyāyana, for whom a word denotes the universal, and Vyāḍi, for whom it denotes the individual. Patañjali’s answer is that Pāṇini accepted both: some of his rules (for example 1.2.58, which allows a plural to refer to a class) presuppose that words denote universals, while others (for example 1.2.64, on the “single remainder” that stands for several individuals) presuppose that they denote individuals.

docs.title: 7.5.4 Correct and incorrect words
docs.text: Patañjali is clear that the incorrect forms are many and the correct few: “each word has many corrupt forms (apabhraṃśa); for the word gauḥ there are gāvī, goṇī, gotā, gopotalikā and so on.” Several of these are recognisable Prakrit forms, so the passage is evidence that Middle Indo-Aryan speech was widespread in his time (Deshpande 1993). He grants that the corrupt forms convey meaning as well as the correct ones; the difference lies in religious merit, not in communication.

docs.title: 7.6 Who Decides What Is Correct?
docs.text:
Grammar, for Patañjali, is ultimately based on usage, but on the usage of a particular group. In discussing rule 6.3.109 he asks how one is to know the correct forms of words not covered by rules, and answers: from the śiṣṭas, the “instructed” or “cultivated”. He defines them as Brahmins of Āryāvarta, the region bounded by the Himalaya and the Pāriyātra hills and lying east of the place where the Sarasvatī disappears and west of the “Black Forest”, who own no more grain than fits in a pot, are free from greed, are virtuous without ulterior motive, and have mastered some branch of learning without being taught. Their usage, not that of other groups, sets the standard (Deshpande 1993).

This definition matters for the social history of Sanskrit. It ties correctness to a male Brahmin elite of a particular region, and it explains why Sanskrit could be described as the language of the śiṣṭas. Madhav Deshpande has shown how, over the following centuries, Sanskrit increasingly became a learned, second language for its users, while the spoken languages developed from the Prakrits; and how grammarians’ attitudes to the vernaculars ranged from contempt to pragmatic acceptance (Deshpande 1993). Sheldon Pollock has traced how Sanskrit, from around the beginning of the Common Era, also became a language of royal inscriptions and courtly literature across South and Southeast Asia (Pollock 2006).

Patañjali was also aware of regional variation. He repeats Yāska’s observation about the Kamboja verb śav “to go” (Chapter 4), and adds that for “to go” the people of Surāṣṭra say hammati and those of the east and centre raṃhati, while the Āryas use gam.

docs.title: 7.6.1 Who learned grammar?
docs.text:
The grammarians’ own examples give glimpses of who studied grammar in their time. Pāṇini’s rules on feminine forms, and Kātyāyana’s notes on them, distinguish the wife of a teacher (ācāryānī, upādhyāyānī) from a woman who is herself a teacher (ācāryā, upādhyāyā or upādhyāyī), and the Mahābhāṣya uses as examples feminine words for women who studied particular grammatical or exegetical works. Such forms would hardly have been needed if no women taught or studied. They suggest that in the last centuries BCE some women of learned Brahmin families were educated in the sciences of language (Deshpande 1993).

The normative literature of the following centuries narrowed these possibilities. The Dharmaśāstras restrict the study of the Veda to men of the three upper varṇas, after initiation; women and Śūdras were excluded, and some texts prescribe harsh punishments for a Śūdra who hears or recites the Veda. Since grammar was justified above all as an auxiliary of the Veda, Sanskrit grammatical learning in the traditional schools was, for most of its history, the preserve of upper-caste, mostly Brahmin, men. There were always exceptions and alternatives. Buddhist and Jain monasteries taught grammar to monks and nuns of varied origin, and their grammarians (Section 5.16 and Chapter 9) produced some of the most widely used grammars of Sanskrit and Pali. Women poets wrote in Sanskrit and the Prakrits, and Sanskrit drama gave women characters Prakrit speech (Chapter 9). In the modern period, reformers and institutions opened Sanskrit learning to all, and Sanskrit and linguistics are now taught in universities without restriction of birth or gender.

Grammar and merit

Patañjali repeatedly links correct speech to religious merit (dharma). He quotes a Vedic saying that a single word correctly known and properly used becomes a wish-granting cow in heaven. Kātyāyana’s first note, as we saw, already justifies grammar by its contribution to dharma. This religious justification coexisted with very practical concerns: correct ritual, the adaptation of mantras, the clear understanding of texts. Later philosophers, above all Bhartṛhari, developed it into a view of grammar as a path to liberation.

docs.title: 7.7 Grammatical Discussions
docs.text: Most of the Mahābhāṣya consists of technical discussion of particular rules, and it is here, rather than in the famous introduction, that Patañjali’s method can be seen at work: on the first rule of the grammar, on compounds, on the exceptions in the kāraka section, and on the principles by which rules are to be read.

docs.title: 7.7.1 The first rule
docs.text: Patañjali’s discussion of the very first rule, vṛddhir ādaic (“ā, ai and au are called vṛddhi”), shows his method in miniature. Why, he asks in his comment on this rule, does Pāṇini put the defined term first and the sounds second, contrary to the order of his other definitions? One answer is auspiciousness: the teacher wished to begin his work with the word vṛddhi, which in ordinary language means “growth, prosperity”, so that the grammar might prosper and its students live long. Patañjali also discusses whether the technical term is needed at all, whether ādaic includes the long vowels, and how a defined term can apply to sounds in rules that come before the definition. The passage mixes the practical, the playful and the theoretical in a way typical of the whole work.

docs.title: 7.7.2 Compounds and their meaning
docs.text: Under rule 2.1.1 (samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ, “a rule concerning words [applies to words] that are semantically connected”) Patañjali discusses what makes a compound such as rājapuruṣa (“king’s man”) possible. On one view the compound’s members acquire a single, unified meaning (ekārthībhāva); on another they simply remain mutually dependent (vyapekṣā), as in the phrase rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ. He shows that the two views have different consequences: for instance, one can say ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ (“the man of the prosperous king”) but not ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ in the same sense, because a member of a compound cannot normally be qualified from outside it.

docs.title: 7.7.3 Kārakas and their exceptions
docs.text: Patañjali examines the many places where Pāṇini’s assignment of kārakas departs from what one might expect from meaning alone. Rule 1.4.46 (adhiśīṅsthāsāṃ karma) treats the place where one lies, stands or sits, after the preverb adhi, as the object rather than the locus: hence grāmam adhiśete “he lies in the village”, with the accusative. Rule 1.4.51 (akathitaṃ ca) treats certain non-specified participants as objects, giving double accusatives such as gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ “he milks milk from the cow”. Such cases show that the kārakas are grammatical categories, defined by the rules, and not simply labels for real-world roles.

docs.title: 7.7.4 Interpretive principles
docs.text:
The Mahābhāṣya discusses many interpretive principles (paribhāṣā) that later grammarians collected, culminating in Nāgeśa’s Paribhāṣenduśekhara. See Table 7.2.

Table 7.2. Some interpretive principles discussed in the Mahābhāṣya Principle Meaning sthānivad ādeśo ’nalvidhau (1.1.56) A substitute behaves like the element it replaces, except in rules concerning individual sounds ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā (1.1.49) A genitive in a rule denotes the element to be replaced yena vidhis tadantasya (1.1.72) A rule stated for an element applies to forms ending in that element pratyayaḥ, paraś ca (3.1.1–2) What is introduced in this section is a suffix, and it follows its base antaraṅgaṃ balīyaḥ An internally conditioned operation is stronger than an externally conditioned one utsargāpavāda A special rule (apavāda) sets aside the general rule (utsarga)

docs.title: 7.8 The Mahābhāṣya as a Historical Source
docs.text: Patañjali’s examples are a valuable source for the history of the 2nd century BCE. Besides the references to Puṣyamitra and the Yavanas, he mentions that the Mauryas, wanting gold, set up images of gods (on rule 5.3.99); he describes performers (śobhikas) who enact the killing of Kaṃsa and the binding of Bali, one of the earliest references to dramatic performance in India (on rule 3.1.26); and he refers to coins such as the kārṣāpaṇa, to trades, food, games and festivals. Agrawala’s study of Pāṇini’s India drew on the same kind of evidence (Agrawala 1953).

docs.title: 7.9 Transmission and Influence
docs.text:
The Mahābhāṣya became the final authority of Pāṇinian grammar. Its later history was not smooth. Bhartṛhari tells, in verses near the end of the second book of his Vākyapadīya (2.484–486), that the tradition of grammar had been lost among Patañjali’s successors and survived among the southerners only as a bare text (granthamātra), until scholars beginning with Candrācārya, having obtained the tradition “from the mountain” (parvatāt), restored it; the Kashmiri chronicle Rājataraṅgiṇī also credits Candrācārya with reviving it. Bhartṛhari himself wrote a commentary on it, the Mahābhāṣyadīpikā, of which only a part survives in a single manuscript (Table 7.3).

Table 7.3. The commentarial chain on the Mahābhāṣya Work Author Date Mahābhāṣya Patañjali mid-2nd c. BCE Mahābhāṣyadīpikā (partly preserved) Bhartṛhari 5th c. CE Pradīpa Kaiyaṭa 11th c. Uddyota (on the Pradīpa) Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa c. 1700

Patañjali’s arguments were known far beyond grammar. Mīmāṃsakas, Naiyāyikas, Vedāntins and Buddhist logicians all engaged with his views on the word, on universals and on the relation between word and meaning. Modern scholarship on the text was transformed by Kielhorn’s critical edition (1880–1885, later revised by K. V. Abhyankar) and by the annotated translations of S. D. Joshi and J. A. F. Roodbergen (Kielhorn 1962–1972; Joshi and Roodbergen 1986).

docs.title: 7.10 Conclusion
docs.text: The Mahābhāṣya turned Pāṇini’s concise rules into a living tradition of argument. It defends the rules where they can be defended, corrects them where it must, and in doing so raises questions that later philosophers of language took up: what a word is, whether it is eternal, whether it denotes a universal or an individual, how compounds mean, and whose usage counts as correct. Its answers to the last question remind us that the science of grammar was also an instrument of social distinction. Its answers to the others make it a founding text of what Bimal Krishna Matilal called India’s contribution to the study of language (Matilal 1990).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:

  • Kielhorn, F., ed. 1962–1972. The Vyākaraṇa-Mahābhāṣya of Patañjali. 3rd ed. Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute.. — The standard edition of the text.

  • Kielhorn, F. 1876. Kātyāyana and Patañjali: Their Relation to Each Other and to Pāṇini. Education Society’s Press.. — On the relation of Kātyāyana and Patañjali.

  • Deshpande, Madhav M. 1993. Sanskrit and Prakrit: Sociolinguistic Issues. Motilal Banarsidass.. — On correctness, the śiṣṭas and the Prakrits.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Bhartṛhari’s Vākyapadīya: The Philosophy of Language
docs.text:
anādinidhanam brahma śabdatattvaṃ yad akṣaram vivartate ’rthabhāvena prakriyā jagato yataḥ The brahman without beginning or end, whose essence is the Word, the imperishable, which appears in the form of things, and from which the world proceeds.

— Vākyapadīya 1.1

docs.title: 8.1 Bhartṛhari
docs.text: Bhartṛhari is the most important philosopher of the Sanskrit grammatical tradition. His Vākyapadīya (“[Treatise] on Sentence and Word”) takes up the questions raised in Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya — what a word is, how it relates to meaning, how sentences convey what they convey — and builds them into a comprehensive philosophy in which language is the fundamental principle of reality (Iyer 1969; Coward and Raja 1990).

docs.title: 8.1.1 Date and identity
docs.text:
Bhartṛhari is now generally dated to the 5th century CE. The decisive evidence is that the Buddhist logician Dignāga (c. 480–540) quotes verses of the Vākyapadīya and was influenced by its ideas; and Bhartṛhari in turn seems unaware of Dignāga. The Chinese pilgrim Yijing, who studied in India in the late 7th century, reported that a famous grammarian named Bhartṛhari had died some forty years earlier, which would place him in the mid-7th century. That report was once widely followed, but it cannot be squared with Dignāga’s quotations and is now thought to rest on confusion with another person or on garbled information. Commentators name Vasurāta as Bhartṛhari’s teacher.

Tradition also identifies the grammarian with Bhartṛhari the poet, author of the three “centuries” of verses on worldly wisdom, love and renunciation (Śatakatraya). Most modern scholars consider the identification doubtful: the name was common, and the poetry is not demonstrably the work of the philosopher.

docs.title: 8.1.2 Works
docs.text:
Bhartṛhari’s main work, the Vākyapadīya, consists of about two thousand verses (kārikā) in three books (kāṇḍa). A prose commentary on the first two books, the Vṛtti, is regarded by most scholars as his own, though this has been disputed. He also wrote a commentary on Patañjali, the Mahābhāṣyadīpikā, of which only an opening portion, covering part of the first quarter of Pāṇini’s first chapter, survives in a single manuscript.

The Vākyapadīya has old commentaries by Vṛṣabhadeva (on the Vṛtti), Puṇyarāja (on the second book) and Helārāja of Kashmir (10th century, on the third book). Modern editions differ in their verse numbering: the critical edition of the verses by Wilhelm Rau (Rau 1977) numbers the first book differently from the edition with the Vṛtti by K. A. Subramania Iyer (Iyer 1965). Verse numbers below follow Rau unless stated otherwise.

docs.title: 8.2 Structure of the Vākyapadīya
docs.text:
The work is divided into three books (Table 8.1).

Table 8.1. The three books of the Vākyapadīya (verse counts vary with the edition) Book Name Verses Subject I Brahmakāṇḍa (also Āgamasamuccaya) c. 150–180 The Word-principle; grammar and tradition; the levels of speech; sphoṭa and sound II Vākyakāṇḍa c. 490 The sentence and its meaning; theories of the sentence; pratibhā III Padakāṇḍa (also Prakīrṇaka) c. 1,325 Fourteen sections (samuddeśa) on the categories of word-meaning

docs.title: 8.3 The Word-Principle (śabdatattva)
docs.text:
The first verse (quoted at the head of this chapter) identifies the ultimate reality, brahman, with the “essence of the Word” (śabdatattva). This brahman is without beginning or end; it “appears” (vivartate) in the form of things, and the world proceeds from it. The second verse adds that this single principle appears as many through its powers:

Vākyapadīya 1.2

ekam eva yad āmnātaṃ bhinnaśaktivyapāśrayāt apṛthaktve ’pi śaktibhyaḥ pṛthaktveneva vartate

“That which is taught as one, resting on its distinct powers, exists as if separate from them, though it is not separate from its powers.”

The chief of these powers is time (kālaśakti), which introduces sequence into what is in itself undivided. The language of vivarta (“appearance”) has invited comparison with Advaita Vedānta, and Bhartṛhari influenced Maṇḍana Miśra and later Advaitins; but scholars warn against reading the later Advaita doctrine of illusion back into him (Coward and Raja 1990; Bronkhorst 2011).

The best-known verse of the first book states the thesis that all cognition is bound up with language:

Vākyapadīya 1.131 (1.123 in Iyer’s edition)

na so ’sti pratyayo loke yaḥ śabdānugamād ṛte anuviddham iva jñānaṃ sarvaṃ śabdena bhāsate

“There is no cognition in the world that is not accompanied by the word; all knowledge appears as if shot through with the word.”

The claim is a strong one: even perception, for Bhartṛhari, carries a latent verbal form. It was rejected by the Buddhist logicians, for whom perception in the strict sense is free of conceptual construction (kalpanāpoḍha, in Dignāga’s definition), and by many Naiyāyikas (Matilal 1990).

Bhartṛhari also gives grammar a soteriological value. In the first book he calls it the door to liberation and the remedy for the impurities of speech: through the knowledge of correct words one comes to understand the Word-principle itself.

docs.title: 8.3.1 Correct and corrupt words
docs.text: Bhartṛhari also takes up Patañjali’s question of correct and incorrect words (Chapter 7). Incorrect forms (apabhraṃśa), he argues, do convey meaning, but only indirectly: hearing a corrupt form, a listener is reminded of the correct word, and it is the correct word that conveys the meaning. He reports two views on the history of language. On one, the “divine speech” was originally correct and was corrupted by speakers unable to pronounce it properly; on the other, held by those who deny that words are eternal, the popular speech is the natural, original language (prakṛti), and correct Sanskrit is a later refinement. Bhartṛhari himself sides with the first view, but the passage shows that the relation between Sanskrit and the Prakrits was already a subject of theoretical reflection in his time (Deshpande 1993).

docs.title: 8.4 The Levels of Speech
docs.text:
In the first book Bhartṛhari describes speech as threefold (trayī vāc):

Paśyantī (“seeing”) Speech in which there is no sequence: the undivided form in which what is to be said exists before it is ordered into words. Madhyamā (“middle”) Speech as it exists in the mind, already ordered in sequence but not yet uttered. Vaikharī (“manifest”) Audible speech produced by the organs of articulation.

A fourth, higher level, parā, was added by later Kashmir Śaiva authors; Figure 1.1 in Chapter 1 shows the three levels together with this later addition.

docs.title: 8.5 The Sphoṭa Theory
docs.text: The term sphoṭa, from the root sphuṭ “to burst, become manifest”, was used by Patañjali for the word as distinct from the sounds that utter it (Chapter 7). Bhartṛhari made it central.

docs.title: 8.5.1 The problem
docs.text: When we hear the word gauḥ we hear the sounds g, au and ḥ one after another, and each has vanished before the next is uttered. Yet we understand the meaning “cow” as a whole. What, then, conveys the meaning? Not any single sound, since none of them alone means “cow”; and not all of them together, since they never exist together.

docs.title: 8.5.2 Bhartṛhari’s answer
docs.text:
The meaning is conveyed by the sphoṭa, a unitary linguistic entity that the sounds (dhvani, nāda) manifest but do not compose. The successive sounds reveal it progressively, each leaving an impression, until with the last sound the whole is grasped. Bhartṛhari distinguishes the “primary” sound (prākṛta dhvani), which is the pattern of sounds characteristic of the word, from the “secondary” features of a particular utterance (vaikṛta dhvani), such as speed, loudness or the speaker’s voice, which do not affect the word’s identity. The distinction has been compared with the modern distinction between the phonological form of a word and its phonetic realisation; the comparison is useful, though the sphoṭa is also, for Bhartṛhari, the bearer of meaning (Figure 8.1).

Figure 8.1. The sphoṭa theory in outline

docs.title: 8.5.3 Word or sentence?
docs.text: The sphoṭa can be discussed at the level of the sound, the word or the sentence. For Bhartṛhari the sentence is the real unit of communication: words and their parts are abstractions extracted from sentences by grammatical analysis (apoddhāra), useful for teaching but not the ultimate bearers of meaning. Much later, Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa (c. 1700) systematised the doctrine into eight kinds of sphoṭa: of the sound, the word and the sentence; of the indivisible word and the indivisible sentence; and of the universals of sound, word and sentence. This eightfold scheme is Nāgeśa’s, not Bhartṛhari’s (Coward and Raja 1990).

docs.title: 8.6 The Sentence (Vākyakāṇḍa)
docs.text:
The second book opens by listing eight views of what a sentence is, held by different schools (Table 8.2).

Table 8.2. Eight views of the sentence listed at the beginning of the second book (2.1–2, in the readings of Rau’s edition) View The sentence is … ākhyāta the verb (since a verb alone can be a complete sentence) śabdasaṃghāta the collection of words jātiḥ saṃghātavartinī a universal residing in the collection of words eko ’navayavaḥ śabdaḥ a single, partless utterance krama the sequence of words buddhyanusaṃhṛti the unified grasp of the words in the mind padam ādyam the first word pṛthak sarvaṃ padaṃ sākāṅkṣam each word, as long as it requires (literally “expects”) the others

The commentator Puṇyarāja groups them into two kinds. Five treat the sentence as made up of parts (the verb, the collection of words, the sequence, the first word, and each word requiring the others); three treat it as a partless unity (the universal residing in the collection, the single partless utterance, and the unified grasp in the mind). Bhartṛhari discusses them all at length. His own view, from the highest standpoint, is that the sentence is a partless unity (akhaṇḍa) and that its meaning is grasped in a single flash of understanding, pratibhā.

docs.title: 8.6.1 Pratibhā
docs.text: Pratibhā (“intuition, flash of understanding”) is the cognition in which the meaning of a sentence is grasped as a whole, and which prompts a hearer to act. Bhartṛhari extends the notion widely: it is pratibhā that tells a bird how to build its nest or a cuckoo when to sing in spring. He lists six sources from which it may arise: nature, conduct, practice, meditation, unseen merit, and the grace of a qualified person. The theory has been compared with Gestalt accounts of perception; its main point, in Bhartṛhari’s own terms, is that understanding a sentence is not a step-by-step inference from the meanings of its words.

docs.title: 8.6.2 Later debates on sentence-meaning
docs.text: Bhartṛhari’s holism was one pole of a long debate. In the 7th century the Mīmāṃsakas developed two influential compositional theories: for Kumārila Bhaṭṭa and his followers, words first express their own meanings, which are then connected into the sentence-meaning (abhihitānvaya); for Prabhākara, words express their meanings only as already related to the other words of the sentence (anvitābhidhāna). Later Naiyāyikas, especially in the Navya-Nyāya school, built a precise account of the cognition produced by a sentence (śābdabodha) on the basis of word-meanings and the conditions of expectancy, compatibility and contiguity (Matilal 1990). The wider doctrines of these schools are treated in Volume 3, Darśana Darpaṇa.

docs.title: 8.7 The Categories of Meaning (Padakāṇḍa)
docs.text:
The third and longest book analyses the categories through which words mean, in fourteen sections (Table 8.3).

Table 8.3. The fourteen sections (samuddeśa) of the third book No. Section Topic 1 Jāti The universal as word-meaning 2 Dravya The substance or individual as word-meaning 3 Sambandha Relation, including the relation of word and meaning 4 Bhūyodravya A short supplement on substance 5 Guṇa Quality 6 Dik Space and direction 7 Sādhana The means of action: the kārakas 8 Kriyā Action 9 Kāla Time 10 Puruṣa Grammatical person 11 Saṅkhyā Number 12 Upagraha The active and middle forms of the verb 13 Liṅga Gender 14 Vṛtti Complex formations: compounds and derivatives

The book turns the categories of the grammar into questions of philosophy. On the old dispute whether words denote universals or individuals, Bhartṛhari follows Patañjali in showing that the grammar can be described on either view, and he treats the choice less as a question of fact than of perspective (Bronkhorst 2011). The relation between a word and its meaning, he argues, cannot itself be expressed as a thing; it is known only through usage, a position that Jan Houben has studied in detail (Houben 1995). The participants in an action, the kārakas, are fixed not by the nature of things but by how the speaker chooses to present them (vivakṣā): the same pot may be presented as the locus (“he cooks in the pot”), the instrument (“he cooks with the pot”) or even the agent (sthālī pacati, “the pot cooks”), which makes the kārakas grammatical-semantic categories rather than physical roles. And time, which in the first book was the chief power of the Word-principle, appears here as the power that orders all things in sequence, like the operator of a machine who sets all its parts in motion.

docs.title: 8.8 Theories of Meaning after Bhartṛhari
docs.text: Bhartṛhari’s work belongs to a much wider debate about meaning that involved grammarians, Mīmāṃsakas, Naiyāyikas, Buddhists and theorists of poetry. Its participants agreed on few answers, but they came to share a vocabulary: how a word’s meaning is learned, how literal, transferred and suggested meanings differ, how a word can apply to many things, and what a sentence finally conveys (Matilal 1990; Coward and Raja 1990).

docs.title: 8.8.1 How the meaning of a word is learned
docs.text: How does one come to know that a word has a particular meaning, its “denotative power” (śakti)? A verse quoted by later Naiyāyikas lists eight means: grammar, comparison, dictionaries, the statement of a reliable person, observation of the usage of elders, the context of a sentence, explanation by synonyms, and proximity to a word whose meaning is already known. The most fundamental is the observation of usage (vyavahāra): a child hears an elder say “bring the cow” and sees another person bring it; hearing “tie up the horse, bring the cow” and seeing the corresponding actions, the child learns by comparison which word goes with which thing. The example, found in many texts, is a simple but serious theory of language acquisition by observation and analysis.

docs.title: 8.8.2 Denotation, indication and suggestion
docs.text:
Indian theorists recognised that words do not always mean what they denote.

Abhidhā (denotation) The primary meaning, learned by convention. Lakṣaṇā (indication) A secondary meaning, invoked when the primary one does not fit. The standard example is gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ, literally “a cowherds’ village on the Ganges”. A village cannot stand on the river itself, so “Ganges” is taken to indicate the bank. Three conditions are usually stated: the primary meaning must be incompatible with the context, the indicated meaning must be connected with it, and there must be either an established usage or a purpose for the indirect expression. Later theorists distinguished kinds of indication. In “a village on the Ganges” the literal meaning is given up entirely (jahallakṣaṇā). In “the lances enter” (kuntāḥ praviśanti), meaning the men carrying lances, the literal meaning is kept and something is added to it (ajahallakṣaṇā). And in “this is that Devadatta” (so ’yaṃ devadattaḥ), said of a man seen before in another place and time, part of each meaning is given up and part kept, so that only the person himself is identified (jahadajahallakṣaṇā). Advaita Vedāntins used this last kind to interpret the sentence tat tvam asi, “you are that”. Vyañjanā (suggestion) A further power, defended by Ānandavardhana (9th century) in the Dhvanyāloka, by which a word or poem conveys a meaning beyond both denotation and indication. In the Ganges example, the expression suggests the coolness and purity of the village, which saying “on the bank” would not. Philosophers such as Mahimabhaṭṭa argued that suggestion could be reduced to inference; the poeticians’ defence of it made dhvani the central concept of Sanskrit literary theory.

docs.title: 8.8.3 The Buddhist theory of exclusion (apoha)
docs.text: Dignāga, who knew Bhartṛhari’s work, accepted some of his insights, notably that a word’s meaning is shaped by the speaker’s conceptual construction, but rejected the existence of real universals. For Dignāga only momentary particulars are real; they are grasped by perception, which is free of concepts. Words and concepts, by contrast, never reach the particular: a word conveys its meaning by excluding what it does not apply to. “Cow” means, in effect, “not a non-cow”. The theory explains how a single word can apply to many individuals without postulating a universal “cowness” that exists in each of them. Dharmakīrti developed it, connecting it with a theory of how concepts arise from the experience of particulars that have similar effects, and later Buddhist philosophers such as Śāntarakṣita and Ratnakīrti refined it further. Mīmāṃsakas, above all Kumārila, and Naiyāyikas attacked it as circular, since the idea of a “non-cow” seems to presuppose the idea of a cow (Matilal 1990). The debate is one of the most sophisticated pre-modern discussions of universals and reference.

docs.title: 8.8.4 What does a sentence mean? (śābdabodha)
docs.text:
In the later tradition the three main schools gave different analyses of the cognition produced by a simple sentence such as caitraḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati (“Caitra cooks rice”), summarised in Table 8.4.

Table 8.4. Three analyses of the cognition produced by “Caitra cooks rice” School Chief qualificand and paraphrase Nyāya The agent, expressed by the word in the nominative: “Caitra, who is the agent of an act of cooking that has rice as its object” Grammarians The action, expressed by the verbal root: “an act of cooking, which has Caitra as agent and rice as object” Mīmāṃsā The productive effort (bhāvanā) expressed by the verbal ending: “an effort, belonging to Caitra, that produces the cooking of rice”

The disagreement may look scholastic, but it concerns a real question that modern semantics also asks: whether the core of a sentence’s meaning is an event, with participants attached, or an entity of which something is predicated. The grammarians’ event-centred view was developed in the 17th and 18th centuries by Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa (Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra) and Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa (Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā), while Navya-Nyāya authors such as Gadādhara refined the logicians’ analysis with great technical precision. It was these analyses, rather than ordinary Sanskrit, that Rick Briggs compared to the knowledge representations of artificial intelligence (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 8.8.5 Grammar and poetics
docs.text: The grammarians’ ideas had a lasting effect on Sanskrit literary theory. Ānandavardhana, defending the theory of suggestion (dhvani) in the 9th century, explicitly modelled his central term on the grammarians’ usage: just as the grammarians call the audible sounds that manifest the sphoṭa dhvani, so poets may call dhvani a poem in which the words and their literal meaning manifest a further, suggested meaning. He described the grammarians as “the first among the learned”. Abhinavagupta’s commentary on Ānandavardhana, and later works on poetics, continued to draw on grammatical and Mīmāṃsā theories of meaning, so that the Sanskrit theory of literature can be read in part as an extension of the philosophy of language described in this chapter (see Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā).

docs.title: 8.9 Responses and Influence
docs.text:
Almost every later school had to take a position on Bhartṛhari. The Buddhists borrowed from him while rejecting his metaphysics, the Mīmāṃsakas and most Naiyāyikas rejected the sphoṭa, and the Kashmir Śaivas and the poeticians absorbed his ideas into systems of their own (Table 8.5).

Table 8.5. Responses to Bhartṛhari’s theories (selected) School Thinker Position Buddhist logic Dignāga, Dharmakīrti Accepted some of his analysis of sentence-meaning and conceptual construction, but rejected the Word-principle and real universals; developed apoha Mīmāṃsā Kumārila Bhaṭṭa Rejected sphoṭa (in the Ślokavārttika): the phonemes themselves, the last one aided by the impressions of the earlier ones, convey the meaning Advaita Vedānta Maṇḍana Miśra Defended sphoṭa in the Sphoṭasiddhi; drew on Bhartṛhari in the Brahmasiddhi Advaita Vedānta Śaṅkara Rejected sphoṭa in his commentary on Brahmasūtra 1.3.28, holding with Upavarṣa that the phonemes alone are the word Nyāya Jayanta Bhaṭṭa Rejected sphoṭa in the Nyāyamañjarī Kashmir Śaivism Somānanda; Utpaladeva; Abhinavagupta Somānanda criticised Bhartṛhari’s paśyantī; Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta absorbed much of his thought into the doctrine of parā vāc Poetics Ānandavardhana; Abhinavagupta Modelled the theory of suggestion (dhvani) partly on the grammarians’ distinction between sound and sphoṭa

The Vākyapadīya was studied mainly in Kashmir and among a small circle of grammarians for many centuries. It was rediscovered by modern scholarship in the 20th century through the work of K. A. Subramania Iyer, Wilhelm Rau, Ashok Aklujkar, Johannes Bronkhorst and others (Iyer 1969; Rau 1977; Chaturvedi 2009). Modern writers have compared Bhartṛhari’s ideas with Wittgenstein’s view of meaning as use, with semantic holism, with the Sapir–Whorf hypothesis that language shapes thought, and with Saussure’s distinction between the linguistic system and individual speech. Such comparisons can be illuminating, but they easily mislead: Bhartṛhari’s concerns were grammatical, ritual and soteriological, and his arguments must be understood first in the context of the Indian debates in which they were made (Matilal 1990; Bronkhorst 2011).

Scholarly Note: Kumārila’s critique of sphoṭa

Kumārila Bhaṭṭa’s Ślokavārttika (7th century) contains a section devoted to refuting the sphoṭa. He argues that postulating an extra, unperceived entity is unnecessary: each phoneme leaves a latent impression (saṃskāra), and the last phoneme, together with the impressions of the earlier ones, produces the cognition of the word and its meaning. The grammarians replied that impressions of separate sounds cannot by themselves explain the unitary grasp of a word. The debate between “phoneme theorists” and “sphoṭa theorists” continued into the 18th century.
