docs.title: Chapter 9: Pali, the Prakrits and Apabhraṃśa: The Middle Indo-Aryan Traditions
docs.text:
saṃskṛtaṃ nāma daivī vāg anvākhyātā maharṣibhiḥ tadbhavas tatsamo deśīty anekaḥ prākṛtakramaḥ Sanskrit is the divine speech, explained by the great sages. Prakrit usage is of several kinds: derived from it, identical with it, and regional.

— Daṇḍin, Kāvyādarśa 1.33

docs.title: 9.1 Introduction
docs.text:
For most of Indian history, most people did not speak Sanskrit. They spoke the languages that linguists call Middle Indo-Aryan (MIA): the Prakrits (prākṛta, “natural, ordinary”), of which Pali is one, and later the Apabhraṃśa languages, from which the modern Indo-Aryan languages developed. These languages have their own literatures, among them the canon of Theravāda Buddhism, the scriptures of the Jains, a rich lyric poetry and much of Indian drama, and their own grammatical traditions. They also form the bulk of the earliest Indian inscriptions, including those of Aśoka (Masica 1991; Salomon 1998). See Table 9.1.

Table 9.1. Stages of Indo-Aryan (dates approximate and overlapping) Stage Period Languages Old Indo-Aryan c. 1500–500 BCE (Vedic); later as a learned language Vedic Sanskrit; Classical Sanskrit Early Middle Indo-Aryan c. 3rd c. BCE – 2nd c. CE Aśokan and other early inscriptional Prakrits; Pali; Gāndhārī Middle Middle Indo-Aryan c. 2nd–6th c. CE Literary Prakrits: Mahārāṣṭrī, Śaurasenī, Māgadhī, Ardhamāgadhī; Paiśācī (known only from grammarians) Late Middle Indo-Aryan c. 6th–12th c. Apabhraṃśa; Avahaṭṭha New Indo-Aryan from c. 10th–12th c. Hindi–Urdu, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Odia, Assamese, Sindhi, Kashmiri, Nepali, Sinhala and others

docs.title: 9.2 What Is a Prakrit?
docs.text:
The word prākṛta can be understood in two ways. Indian grammarians derived it from prakṛti “source, base”, and took the base to be Sanskrit: Hemacandra explains that Prakrit is “what arises from, or comes from” Sanskrit, which is its prakṛti. On this view Prakrits are Sanskrit transformed, and the grammarians accordingly describe them by rules that convert Sanskrit forms into Prakrit ones. The word can also mean “natural, common”, and some Prakrit writers, especially Jain authors, took Prakrit to be the natural speech of the people, of which Sanskrit is a refined form.

Modern historical linguistics takes a third view. The Prakrits do not descend from Classical Sanskrit as described by Pāṇini; they descend from spoken Old Indo-Aryan dialects related to, but not identical with, the language of the Vedas and of Pāṇini. Some Prakrit forms preserve features that Sanskrit had lost (Masica 1991; Oberlies 2001). Daṇḍin’s threefold classification, quoted at the head of this chapter, remains useful for vocabulary: tatsama words identical with Sanskrit, tadbhava words derived from Old Indo-Aryan through regular sound change, and deśī words of other origin, many of them from Dravidian or Munda sources.

docs.title: 9.3 Pali
docs.text: Pali is the language of the Theravāda Buddhist canon, the Tipiṭaka (“three baskets”): the Vinaya (monastic discipline), the Sutta (discourses) and the Abhidhamma (systematic doctrine). According to the Sri Lankan chronicles, the canon was written down in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BCE, after centuries of oral transmission.

docs.title: 9.3.1 Name and origin
docs.text: The word pāli originally meant “a line, a text”, specifically the canonical text as opposed to the commentary; its use as the name of a language is late. The Theravāda tradition identifies the language with Māgadhī, the language of Magadha in which the Buddha was believed to have taught. Linguistic study shows that Pali is not the Māgadhī known from inscriptions and grammarians: it shares many features with the western inscriptional Prakrits and shows traces of an eastern substratum, as one would expect of a literary language formed from the transmission of teachings across regions (Norman 1983; Oberlies 2001).

docs.title: 9.3.2 Sound changes
docs.text:
Pali differs from Sanskrit less in its grammar than in its sounds, and the differences are regular enough that a reader of Sanskrit soon learns to see the Sanskrit word behind the Pali one (Table 9.2).

Table 9.2. Some regular correspondences between Sanskrit and Pali Change Sanskrit Pali Assimilation of consonant clusters dharma, karma, putra dhamma, kamma, putta Cluster with r assimilated, aspiration kept artha attha Long vowel shortened before a double consonant sūtra sutta Cluster rv > bb nirvāṇa nibbāna kṣ > kkh (or cch) bhikṣu, kṣetra bhikkhu, khetta Sibilants merged as s śānti, puruṣa santi, purisa Final -aḥ > -o puruṣaḥ puriso Vowel ṛ replaced by a, i or u ṛṣi, vṛkṣa isi, rukkha Table 9.3. The masculine a-stem in Sanskrit and Pali (selected forms) Case Skt. sg. Pali sg. Skt. pl. Pali pl. Nominative devaḥ devo devāḥ devā Accusative devam devaṃ devān deve Instrumental devena devena devaiḥ devehi, devebhi Dative devāya devāya, devassa devebhyaḥ devānaṃ Ablative devāt devā, devasmā, devamhā devebhyaḥ devehi, devebhi Genitive devasya devassa devānām devānaṃ Locative deve deve, devasmiṃ, devamhi deveṣu devesu

Table 9.3 shows the typical Middle Indo-Aryan simplifications: the dative is largely replaced by the genitive, the dual is lost, and pronominal endings (-smā, -smiṃ) spread to nouns.

The first verse of the Dhammapada, one of the best-known texts of the Pali canon, shows many of these features at once:

Dhammapada 1

manopubbaṅgamā dhammā manoseṭṭhā manomayā manasā ce paduṭṭhena bhāsati vā karoti vā tato naṃ dukkham anveti cakkaṃ va vahato padaṃ

“Mental states are preceded by mind, have mind as their chief, are made by mind. If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, suffering follows one, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the cart.”

Compared with Sanskrit, dhammā stands for dharmāḥ, -pubbaṅgamā for -pūrvaṃgamāḥ (with rv > bb and the vowel shortened before the double consonant), seṭṭhā for śreṣṭhāḥ, paduṭṭhena for praduṣṭena, dukkham for duḥkham and cakkaṃ for cakram. A reader who knows Sanskrit can follow the verse almost word for word, which is one reason why Pali has always been studied alongside Sanskrit in India and Sri Lanka.

docs.title: 9.3.3 Pali grammars
docs.text: A Pali grammatical tradition developed in Sri Lanka and Burma, modelled partly on Sanskrit grammars, especially the Kātantra and Pāṇini, but adapted to Pali. The earliest surviving Pali grammar, the Kaccāyanavyākaraṇa, is attributed by tradition to the Buddha’s disciple Kaccāna but is certainly much later (perhaps 6th–8th century; the date is disputed). In 12th-century Sri Lanka Moggallāna wrote a fresh and more systematic grammar, the Saddalakkhaṇa, drawing on the Cāndra grammar of Sanskrit, and in 1154 Aggavaṃsa completed at Pagan in Burma the Saddanīti, the most comprehensive of all Pali grammars. Buddhappiya’s Rūpasiddhi (perhaps 13th century) reworked Kaccāyana for students (Hinüber 1996).

docs.title: 9.3.4 Pali literature beyond the canon
docs.text: Pali literature did not end with the canon. The Milindapañha, a layered work of perhaps the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE, presents the monk Nāgasena answering the questions of King Milinda, the Indo-Greek Menander. Sri Lanka produced chronicles of its own history, the Dīpavaṃsa (4th century) and the Mahāvaṃsa ascribed to Mahānāma (5th–6th century). Above all, Buddhaghosa in the 5th century gave Theravāda its classic manual of doctrine and meditation, the Visuddhimagga, and with his successors wrote the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) through which the canon has been read ever since, including the prose frame of the Jātaka stories. Anuruddha’s Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha (c. 10th–12th century) became the standard short manual of Abhidhamma (Norman 1983; Hinüber 1996).

docs.title: 9.4 The Inscriptional Prakrits
docs.text:
The edicts of Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) are the earliest securely dated Indian texts (Figure 9.1). They are written in several dialects of Prakrit: an eastern one, close to the language of the Mauryan court at Pāṭaliputra, adapted to local speech in different regions, so that the versions at Girnar in the west and at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra in the north-west show western and north-western features (Salomon 1998). Even the king’s titles show the difference: in the eastern versions the epithet “Beloved of the Gods” ends in -e (devānaṃpiye) and “king” is lājā, with l for r, while the Girnar version has the ending -o and the form rājā. The features that the grammarians later attributed to Māgadhī can thus already be seen in the eastern inscriptions of the 3rd century BCE. For several centuries afterwards almost all Indian inscriptions were in Prakrit; Sanskrit began to be used in inscriptions only from around the turn of the Common Era (the Junāgaḍh inscription of Rudradāman, 150 CE, is an early long example), and became the dominant inscriptional language from the 4th century (Pollock 2006). In the north-west a distinct Prakrit, Gāndhārī, written in Kharoṣṭhī script, was the language of administration and of an important Buddhist literature, recovered in recent decades from manuscripts found in Afghanistan and Pakistan (Chapter 12).

Figure 9.1. Aśoka’s inscription on the pillar at Nigali Sagar (Nepal), in Brāhmī script and an eastern Prakrit, reproduced from an early facsimile Plate: Eugen Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka (Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, 1925), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 9.4.1 Sri Lanka and the Maldives
docs.text:
Indo-Aryan speech was carried to Sri Lanka in the 1st millennium BCE. The earliest inscriptions of the island, short Buddhist donative records in Brāhmī from about the 3rd–2nd centuries BCE, are written in a Prakrit that developed into Sinhala; Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives, is closely related. These “insular” Indo-Aryan languages developed in isolation from the mainland and in contact with Tamil, and they show distinctive changes such as the loss of aspiration. Pali, the language of the island’s Buddhist scriptures, coexisted with them as a learned language, much as Sanskrit coexisted with the Prakrits on the mainland.

Sinhala also acquired a grammatical tradition of its own. Its classic is the Sidat Saṅgarāva, a grammar of the literary language (Eḷu or Hela) composed in the 13th century and traditionally attributed to a monk named Vēdēha. It is written in Sinhala and applies to it the categories of the Pali and Sanskrit grammars studied in the island’s monasteries, treating in turn the letters, their combination, nouns and their cases, and verbs. As with the Dravidian grammars (Chapter 11), a borrowed framework had to be adapted to a language that had moved far from its ancestor and had long been in contact with Tamil. The Sidat Saṅgarāva remained the authority for correct literary Sinhala into the modern period, and it was translated into English by James De Alwis in 1852.

docs.title: 9.5 Buddhist Languages: Gāndhārī and Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit
docs.text:
The Buddha is reported in the Pali Vinaya to have told his monks to learn his teaching “in their own language” (sakāya niruttiyā), refusing a proposal to put it into Vedic verse; the phrase has been interpreted both as “in the monk’s own dialect” and as “in the Buddha’s own language”, but on either reading early Buddhism did not treat any one language as sacred. Buddhist texts were accordingly transmitted in several Middle Indo-Aryan languages. Pali is the one whose canon survives complete. In the north-west the texts were transmitted in Gāndhārī, written in Kharoṣṭhī; the discovery since the 1990s of birch-bark manuscripts in Gāndhārī, some dated by radiocarbon to the 1st century CE or earlier, has transformed the study of early Buddhist literature.

From around the beginning of the Common Era, Buddhist schools of northern India, and the Mahāyāna, increasingly adopted Sanskrit. Many texts were composed in, or converted into, a language that mixes Sanskrit and Middle Indo-Aryan forms, which Franklin Edgerton called “Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit” and described in a grammar and dictionary (Edgerton 1953). The gradual Sanskritisation of Buddhist and later of Jain writing is part of the larger movement by which Sanskrit became, in the first millennium CE, the shared language of learning and political expression across South Asia (Pollock 2006).

docs.title: 9.6 Jain Prakrit Literature
docs.text: The Jains preserved the largest body of Prakrit literature. The Śvetāmbara canon, in Ardhamāgadhī, comprises the eleven surviving Aṅgas and numerous further texts, with Prakrit commentaries (niryukti, bhāṣya, cūrṇi) and later Sanskrit ones. The Digambaras regard the old canon as lost and hold as authoritative works in Jain Śaurasenī, such as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and the writings of Kundakunda. Jain authors also wrote a vast secular and narrative literature in Mahārāṣṭrī and Apabhraṃśa: romances, epics, story collections and didactic works. It was largely in the service of this literature that Jain scholars such as Hemacandra wrote grammars, lexicons and works on metre covering Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa alongside Sanskrit.

docs.title: 9.7.1 Prakrit in Sanskrit drama
docs.text:
In Sanskrit drama, by the convention set out in the Nāṭyaśāstra, characters speak different languages according to their gender and status. Kings, Brahmins and other high-status men speak Sanskrit; women, children and most other characters speak Prakrit. The convention mirrored, and reinforced, a social hierarchy in which Sanskrit was the language of high-status men (Table 9.4).

Table 9.4. The principal literary Prakrits Prakrit Region named Use Śaurasenī Śūrasena (Mathurā) The main prose Prakrit of drama, spoken by heroines and other respectable characters; also the language of Digambara Jain scripture Mahārāṣṭrī Mahārāṣṭra The Prakrit of lyric poetry and of songs in drama; Hāla’s anthology; Prakrit epics Māgadhī Magadha Spoken by low-status characters in drama Ardhamāgadhī “half-Māgadhī” The language of the Śvetāmbara Jain canon Paiśācī “of the Piśācas” Language of Guṇāḍhya’s lost Bṛhatkathā; known only from grammarians and quotations

docs.title: 9.7.2 Mahārāṣṭrī
docs.text:
Mahārāṣṭrī was considered the Prakrit par excellence for poetry. Its most famous work is the Gāhāsattasaī (Sanskrit Gāthāsaptaśatī), “Seven Hundred Verses”, an anthology of short love poems attributed to the Sātavāhana king Hāla. The anthology probably took shape in the early centuries CE, with later additions; its verses, many spoken in the voices of village women, are among the finest lyrics of ancient India. Mahārāṣṭrī is characterised by the loss of single consonants between vowels: Sanskrit nagara “town” becomes ṇaara, loka “world” becomes loa.

Prakrit poetry was not merely a lower register of Sanskrit (Ollett 2017). Sanskrit poeticians themselves, from Ānandavardhana onwards, quoted Prakrit stanzas from Hāla’s anthology as model examples of suggestion (dhvani), and Prakrit court epics such as Pravarasena’s Setubandha (on the building of Rāma’s bridge, 5th century) and Vākpati’s Gauḍavaho (8th century) show that Mahārāṣṭrī was a prestigious literary medium. Rājaśekhara’s Karpūramañjarī (c. 900) is a whole play in Prakrit. The ideal of the poet who commands both Sanskrit and Prakrit, and often Apabhraṃśa and Paiśācī as well, was widespread in the courts of the late 1st millennium.

docs.title: 9.7.3 Śaurasenī
docs.text: Śaurasenī keeps a voiced form of dental stops between vowels where Mahārāṣṭrī loses them: Sanskrit gacchati “goes” becomes Śaurasenī gacchadi but Mahārāṣṭrī gacchaï. The western New Indo-Aryan languages, including the ancestor of Hindi, are often traced to the Apabhraṃśa of the Śaurasenī region, but the descent of the modern languages from particular literary Prakrits is a simplification (Masica 1991).

docs.title: 9.7.4 Māgadhī and Ardhamāgadhī
docs.text: Māgadhī, as described by the grammarians and used in drama, has ś for every sibilant, l for r, and the nominative singular ending -e instead of -o: Sanskrit rājā “king” becomes lājā, and puruṣaḥ “man” becomes puliśe. Ardhamāgadhī, the language of the Śvetāmbara Jain canon (the Āgamas), shares the ending -e but keeps r and s. The Jain canon was fixed at councils, the last of which, at Valabhī, is traditionally dated to the 5th century CE.

docs.title: 9.8 Prakrit Sound Changes
docs.text:
Table 9.5 lists the characteristic sound changes from Old to Middle Indo-Aryan, and Figure 9.2 places them in the longer history of Indo-Aryan.

Table 9.5. Characteristic sound changes from Old to Middle Indo-Aryan Process Sanskrit Prakrit Assimilation of clusters dharma, hasta, bhakta dhamma, hattha, bhatta Loss of single stops between vowels (Mahārāṣṭrī) nagara, loka ṇaara, loa Voicing of t between vowels (Śaurasenī) gacchati gacchadi Aspirated stops between vowels reduced to h mukha, kathā muha, kahā Initial and medial n > ṇ nagara ṇaara Sibilants merged śaśin sasi (Māgadhī śaśi) r > l (Māgadhī) rājā lājā ṛ > a, i, u ghṛta, ṛṣi, vṛkṣa ghaa, isi, rukkha kṣ > kkh or cch kṣetra khetta, chetta Figure 9.2. Stages in the history of Indo-Aryan (simplified; the stages overlap, and each line of descent runs through spoken dialects, not through the literary languages)

docs.title: 9.9 The Prakrit Grammarians
docs.text:
The oldest surviving Prakrit grammar is Vararuci’s Prākṛtaprakāśa, perhaps of the 4th–6th century, with a commentary by Bhāmaha. It takes Mahārāṣṭrī as the Prakrit proper and treats Paiśācī, Māgadhī and Śaurasenī in short chapters of their own. Hemacandra’s eighth chapter (12th century) is the fullest of the grammars and the only one to describe Apabhraṃśa at length, with the many quoted verses mentioned below; Trivikrama’s Prākṛtaśabdānuśāsana (13th century) follows it closely. The later works, such as the Prakrit section of Kramadīśvara’s Saṃkṣiptasāra (c. 13th century), Lakṣmīdhara’s Ṣaḍbhāṣācandrikā on “six languages” (16th century) and Mārkaṇḍeya’s Prākṛtasarvasva (17th century), which represents an eastern school, were written for poets and readers who used the Prakrits as literary languages, above all in drama, long after they had ceased to be spoken.

The Prakrit grammarians describe their languages by stating how a Sanskrit form is transformed into the corresponding Prakrit one. Their rules are therefore systematic correspondences between two languages, not historical sound laws; but they record, accurately and in detail, the regular relationships that 19th-century historical linguists later explained as the results of sound change. Richard Pischel’s Grammatik der Prakrit-Sprachen (1900) built on them and remains the standard reference (Pischel 1900).

docs.title: 9.10 Apabhraṃśa
docs.text:
Apabhraṃśa (“falling away”) was originally a grammarians’ term for any deviant form (Patañjali uses it for incorrect words, Chapter 7). From about the 6th century it became the name of a literary language, or group of languages, representing the last stage of Middle Indo-Aryan. Far from being a corruption, it was the vehicle of a large literature, especially among the Jains (Masica 1991). Svayambhū’s Paümacariu (9th century) is a Jain Rāmāyaṇa and Puṣpadanta’s Mahāpurāṇa (10th century) a Jain universal history, while Dhanapāla’s Bhavisattakaha (10th century) and Kanakāmara’s Karakaṇḍacariu (11th century) are narrative poems. Not all of it is Jain. The Saṃdeśarāsaka, a messenger poem of perhaps the 12th century, is the work of a Muslim poet of the north-west, Abdul Rahmān (Addahamāṇa), and the love and heroic verses that Hemacandra quotes as examples in his grammar come from a popular poetry that is otherwise lost.

The Kuvalayamālā of Uddyotanasūri (779 CE), a Prakrit romance, contains a famous passage in which merchants from eighteen regions of India are each characterised by a few words of their own speech, a rare early record of regional languages. The Buddhist Caryāpadas of eastern India, of uncertain date (perhaps 10th–12th century), are claimed as the earliest literature of Bengali, Assamese, Odia and Maithili.

docs.title: 9.10.1 From Apabhraṃśa to the modern languages
docs.text:
Apabhraṃśa shows many of the features of the modern Indo-Aryan languages: case endings reduced to a few, the growth of postpositions to express case relations, new verbal constructions built on participles, and new pronouns. The New Indo-Aryan languages emerged from the regional speech of this period, and their earliest texts appear from around the 10th to the 13th centuries. Their literatures are surveyed in Volume 8 of this series, Kāvya Kalpalatā.

One regular change in the passage to the modern languages can be followed across all three stages (Table 9.6). Middle Indo-Aryan assimilated the consonant clusters of Old Indo-Aryan into double consonants; New Indo-Aryan then simplified the double consonant and, in compensation, lengthened the vowel before it. Many of the commonest words of Hindi are inherited in this way (tadbhava words), while their Sanskrit originals were later borrowed again as learned words (tatsama), so that Hindi has both kām “work” and karma “action, karma”, both hāth “hand” and hasta in learned compounds.

Table 9.6. Some words through three stages of Indo-Aryan Sanskrit Pali / Prakrit Hindi Meaning hasta hattha hāth hand karma kamma kām work sapta satta sāt seven dugdha duddha dūdh milk agni aggi āg fire karṇa kaṇṇa kān ear

docs.title: 9.11 The First Descriptions of the New Indo-Aryan Languages
docs.text:
The modern Indo-Aryan languages were written long before anyone wrote a grammar of them, and their first descriptions came by roundabout routes. The earliest is a by-product of teaching Sanskrit. Paṇḍita Dāmodara’s Uktivyaktiprakaraṇa, written in the 12th century at the court of the Gāhaḍavāla king Govindacandra, whose capitals were Kanauj and Vārāṇasī, teaches Sanskrit to speakers of the local vernacular, an early form of the language of Kosala (Old Awadhi), by setting vernacular sentences beside their Sanskrit equivalents and explaining Sanskrit constructions through them. It is not a grammar of the vernacular, but in order to teach Sanskrit it has to show how the vernacular expresses case, tense and voice, and so it is the oldest systematic record of an early Hindi dialect. Muni Jinavijaya edited it in 1953 with a linguistic study by Suniti Kumar Chatterji. Later manuals of the same kind, called auktika after this text, taught Sanskrit through Old Gujarati and other vernaculars.

Other early records come from the margins of other sciences. Sarvānanda’s Bengali glosses on the Amarakośa (1159; Section 4.8) are among the earliest evidence for Bengali words, and the Prākṛtapaiṅgala (Section 3.6) preserves verses in the late Apabhraṃśa from which the vernaculars were emerging. Persian scholarship supplied the first grammar of Braj, the literary language of north Indian poetry, in Mīrzā Khān’s Tuḥfat al-Hind (c. 1675), which is described, with the Persian–Hindavi glossaries, in Chapter 13.

European missionaries began to write grammars of the coastal languages in the 17th century. The English Jesuit Thomas Stephens (d. 1619), who worked in Goa, wrote a grammar of Konkani in Portuguese, the Arte da lingoa Canarim, printed in 1640; he is also remembered for a long Christian poem in Marathi, the Kristapurāṇa. The Portuguese Augustinian Manoel da Assumpção published at Lisbon in 1743 a Vocabulario em idioma Bengalla, e Portuguez, with a short grammar of Bengali, and Dutch and German grammars of Hindustani appeared in the same decades (Section 13.6). These works were written for missionaries and traders, in Roman script and on Latin models, and Indian scholars long ignored them; but they are the first grammars of these languages in the European sense, and they precede by a century or more the colonial grammars, such as N. B. Halhed’s Grammar of the Bengal Language (1778), that are often treated as the beginning of the subject. Marathi, Gujarati, Odia and most other languages of the region received their first printed grammars only in the 19th century, from missionaries, colonial officials and, increasingly, Indian scholars (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 9.12 Modern Study
docs.text: The modern study of Pali and the Prakrits began in the 19th century. The Pali Text Society, founded in London by T. W. Rhys Davids in 1881, edited and translated the Pali canon and its commentaries, while in Sri Lanka, Burma and Thailand the canon continued to be studied and recited in the traditional way. Richard Pischel’s grammar of the Prakrits (1900) gathered the evidence of the grammarians, the dramas and the Jain texts (Pischel 1900), and Wilhelm Geiger’s work on Pali and on the Sri Lankan chronicles set the study of Pali on a philological footing. More recent work has emphasised the variety of Middle Indo-Aryan, its inscriptional record and its relation to the modern languages (Oberlies 2001; Norman 1983; Masica 1991). In 2024 the Government of India added Pali and Prakrit, together with Marathi, Bengali and Assamese, to its list of “classical languages”.

docs.title: 9.13 The Place of Middle Indo-Aryan
docs.text: The Middle Indo-Aryan languages fill the two thousand years between the Vedic hymns and the modern languages, and without them the history of Indo-Aryan could not be written. They carry two of the great scriptural canons of India, the Theravāda canon in Pali and the Jain canon in Ardhamāgadhī and Śaurasenī. They are the languages of a major literature, from Prakrit lyric to Apabhraṃśa narrative and the Prakrit passages of drama, and of almost all early Indian inscriptions, including every edict of Aśoka except the Greek and Aramaic versions in the north-west. And the long coexistence of Sanskrit and Prakrit, with its conventions about who spoke which, is some of the best evidence we have for the social history of language in India (Deshpande 1993; Ollett 2017).

docs.text:

  • Oberlies, Thomas. 2001. Pāli: A Grammar of the Language of the Theravāda Tipiṭaka. Walter de Gruyter.. — A modern grammar of Pali.

  • Norman, K. R. 1983. Pāli Literature. A History of Indian Literature, 7.2. Otto Harrassowitz.. — A history of Pali literature.

docs.title: Chapter 10: The Tolkāppiyam: Tamil Grammar and Poetics
docs.text:
akara mutala eḻuttellām āti pakavaṉ mutaṟṟē ulaku As the letter a is the first of all letters, so the world has the primal Lord as its first.

— Tirukkuṟaḷ 1

docs.title: 10.1 Introduction
docs.text: Beside the Sanskrit tradition, India possesses a second ancient tradition of grammatical analysis, that of Tamil. Its foundational text, the Tolkāppiyam, attributed to Tolkāppiyar, is traditionally regarded as the oldest surviving work of Tamil literature, although only its earliest layers may be as old as the oldest Caṅkam poems; it is the earliest grammar of any Dravidian language. It knows the Sanskrit tradition and uses some of its ideas, but it builds a framework of its own, suited to a language of a quite different family and type, and it extends grammar to include a theory of poetry (Zvelebil 1973, 1992). This chapter is devoted to the Tolkāppiyam itself; the later grammars of Tamil and of the other Dravidian languages, and the discovery of the Dravidian family, are the subject of Chapter 11.

docs.title: 10.2 Author, Date and Layers
docs.text:
Nothing certain is known of Tolkāppiyar. The preface (pāyiram) to the work, attributed to his fellow-student Paṉampāraṉār, says that it was presented in the assembly of a Pāṇṭiya king called Nilantaru Tiruviṉ Pāṇṭiyaṉ, before the scholar Ataṅkōṭṭāciriyar, and describes Tolkāppiyar as “full of the Aindra”, that is, versed in the Aindra school of Sanskrit grammar, a tradition known by name but not otherwise preserved. Later commentators made him a disciple of the sage Agastya.

The date of the Tolkāppiyam is much debated, and the work is almost certainly layered. Many scholars place the core of its first two books, on sounds and words, in the last centuries BCE or the early centuries CE; the third book, the Poruḷatikāram, which presupposes a developed body of Caṅkam poetry, is generally considered a later layer, perhaps of the 4th–5th century CE (Zvelebil 1973; Takahashi 1995). Some scholars date the whole work later still. Much earlier dates, reaching back many centuries or even millennia before the Common Era, are sometimes asserted in popular writing; they rest on a medieval legend of three successive Tamil academies (caṅkam) at Madurai, lasting thousands of years (Section 11.2), rather than on evidence.

docs.title: 10.3 Structure
docs.text:
The Tolkāppiyam consists of three books (atikāram), each of nine chapters (iyal), in the short verse lines called nūṟpā. See Table 10.1.

Table 10.1. The three books of the Tolkāppiyam (rule counts following the commentator Iḷampūraṇar) Book Name Rules Subject I Eḻuttatikāram 483 “Letters”: the sounds of Tamil, their classification, distribution and combination (sandhi) II Collatikāram 463 “Words”: word classes, gender, case, the verb, syntax and usage III Poruḷatikāram 656 “Subject-matter”: the themes and conventions of poetry, prosody and rhetoric

The commentaries are essential for understanding the text. The oldest complete one is that of Iḷampūraṇar (perhaps 11th–12th century); others are by Cēṉāvaraiyar (on the second book), Pērāciriyar and Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar (14th century).

docs.title: 10.4.1 The sounds of Tamil
docs.text:
The Tolkāppiyam recognises thirty primary “letters” (mutaleḻuttu): twelve vowels (uyir, “life”) and eighteen consonants (mey, “body”), together with three dependent sounds (cārpeḻuttu): the āytam (written with three dots, transliterated ḵ), and the shortened i and u (kuṟṟiyalikaram, kuṟṟiyalukaram) that occur in certain positions. A consonant combined with a vowel forms a syllable (uyirmey, “life-body”). The very first rule of the work states this count: the letters, it says, are thirty, running from a to ṉ, apart from the three that occur only in dependence on others. The order from a to ṉ is the traditional Tamil order of the letters, which, like the Sanskrit order, begins with the vowels and arranges the consonants partly by class (Table 10.2).

Table 10.2. The primary sounds of Tamil according to the Tolkāppiyam Class Tamil term Sounds Short vowels kuṟil a, i, u, e, o Long vowels neṭil ā, ī, ū, ē, ai, ō, au “Hard” consonants (stops) valliṉam k, c, ṭ, t, p, ṟ “Soft” consonants (nasals) melliṉam ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, m, ṉ “Middle” consonants iṭaiyiṉam y, r, l, v, ḻ, ḷ Dependent sounds cārpeḻuttu āytam (ḵ); shortened i and u

The analysis fits Tamil closely. Tamil distinguishes short and long e and o, which Sanskrit does not; it has no separate voiced or aspirated stops, the voiced pronunciations of k, c, ṭ, t, p being predictable from their position; and it has the retroflex approximant ḻ and the alveolar ṟ and ṉ, which Sanskrit lacks. The threefold grouping of the consonants into hard, soft and middle classes is the basis of the rules of combination.

docs.title: 10.4.2 Combination (puṇarcci)
docs.text: Much of the first book deals with the changes that take place when words or morphemes combine (puṇarcci, “union”). The Tolkāppiyam distinguishes combination without change (iyalpu) from combination with change (tiripu), and describes the insertion, deletion and alteration of sounds at the junction. The doubling of an initial hard consonant after certain words, characteristic of Tamil, is one of its central topics.

docs.title: 10.5.1 Word classes
docs.text:
The Tolkāppiyam divides words into four classes (Table 10.3).

Table 10.3. The four word classes of the Tolkāppiyam Tamil term Approximate equivalent Description peyar noun Names, including pronouns; inflected for case viṉai verb Words expressing action, inflected for tense and person iṭai particle “Intermediate” words: case markers, connectives, clitics uri qualifier “Proper” words, mostly qualitative roots used to qualify nouns and verbs

The fourfold division recalls Yāska’s four classes (noun, verb, preverb, particle; Chapter 4), and the Tolkāppiyam may have been influenced by the Sanskrit tradition. But the classes are not the same: Tamil has no preverbs, and the uri class has no exact Sanskrit counterpart.

docs.title: 10.5.2 Gender: “high” and “non-high” class
docs.text: One of the most distinctive features of Tamil grammar, clearly described in the Tolkāppiyam, is the division of nouns into two classes: uyartiṇai (“high class”), comprising human beings (and gods), and aḵṟiṇai (“non-high class”), comprising everything else. Within the high class, verbs and pronouns distinguish masculine, feminine and plural; within the non-high class, singular and plural. Grammatical gender in Tamil thus follows meaning, unlike gender in Sanskrit, where “wife” may be masculine (dāra) or neuter (kalatra).

docs.title: 10.5.3 Case
docs.text:
The Tolkāppiyam recognises eight cases (vēṟṟumai), numbered like the Sanskrit cases and including the vocative, but expressed by suffixes attached to an invariant stem (Table 10.4).

Table 10.4. The cases in the Tolkāppiyam (markers of Old Tamil) No. Name Marker Function 1 eḻuvāy – (bare stem) Subject 2 second case -ai Object 3 third case -oṭu, -āṉ Accompaniment; instrument 4 fourth case -ku Recipient, purpose 5 fifth case -iṉ Source, comparison 6 sixth case -atu Possession 7 seventh case -kaṇ Location 8 viḷi change of the final Address

Modern Tamil uses different markers for several cases (instrumental -āl, locative -il, ablative -iliruntu), developed after the period of the Tolkāppiyam. Because Tamil suffixes are added to a stem one after another without fusing with it, Tamil morphology is described as agglutinative, in contrast with the fusional morphology of Sanskrit.

docs.title: 10.5.4 The verb
docs.text: The Tamil verb is formed by adding to the stem a tense marker and then a suffix of person, number and gender: paṭi-tt-āṉ “he studied”, paṭi-pp-āṉ “he will study”. (The modern present-tense marker -kiṟ-, as in paṭi-kkiṟ-āṉ “he studies”, is a later development: Old Tamil verb forms mark only past and non-past, although the Tolkāppiyam names three times, past, present and future.) The Tolkāppiyam also describes the participles (eccam) that stand where other languages use relative clauses, and the verbal forms that end a sentence (muṟṟu).

docs.title: 10.5.5 Tamil and Sanskrit grammatical terms
docs.text:
The Tamil tradition has its own technical vocabulary, partly parallel to the Sanskrit one. Some correspondences are close; others hide real differences of analysis (Table 10.5).

Table 10.5. Some Tamil grammatical terms and their nearest Sanskrit counterparts Tamil Sanskrit Notes eḻuttu varṇa, akṣara “Letter”: both sound and written sign uyir svara Vowel (“life”) mey vyañjana Consonant (“body”) col pada, śabda Word poruḷ artha Meaning; subject-matter peyar nāman Noun viṉai kriyā, ākhyāta Verb, action vēṟṟumai vibhakti Case (“difference”) puṇarcci sandhi Combination of sounds tiṇai no exact equivalent Class of nouns (uyartiṇai, aḵṟiṇai); also poetic situation

docs.title: 10.6 The Book of Subject-Matter (Poruḷatikāram)
docs.text:
The third book, which as noted is probably a later layer, makes the Tolkāppiyam unusual among grammars: it is a theory of poetry. It divides poetic subject-matter into akam (“interior”), the poetry of love, and puṟam (“exterior”), the poetry of war, kingship, generosity and death. The conventions it describes are those of the anthologies of Caṅkam poetry (Zvelebil 1973; Ramanujan 1967), whose literature is treated in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā; this chapter is concerned with the theory.

The poems to which these conventions apply are preserved in two great collections, together known as the Caṅkam (or Saṅgam) literature: the “Eight Anthologies” (Eṭṭuttokai), which include the Kuṟuntokai, Naṟṟiṇai, Akanāṉūṟu, Aiṅkuṟunūṟu and Kalittokai (love poetry) and the Puṟanāṉūṟu and Patiṟṟuppattu (heroic poetry), and the “Ten Songs” (Pattuppāṭṭu), longer poems. Most of the poems are generally dated to the first three centuries CE, though the collections were compiled later. They were largely forgotten for centuries and were rediscovered and printed in the late 19th century, above all through the work of U. Vē. Cāminātaiyar, who searched out and edited the palm-leaf manuscripts (Figure 10.1). Eva Wilden has traced how fragile that transmission was, and how much of the Caṅkam corpus survived in only a handful of copies (Zvelebil 1973; Wilden 2014).

Figure 10.1. Two leaves of a palm-leaf manuscript in a South Indian script; texts such as the Tolkāppiyam and its commentaries were transmitted in manuscripts of this kind until they were printed in the 19th century Photo: Ms Sarah Welch, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Scholarly Note: Gender and caste in the Poruḷatikāram

The Poruḷatikāram codifies a poetic world with clear social boundaries. Its rules specify which characters may speak in which situations: the heroine, her friend, her foster-mother, the hero and his companions, the courtesan. It discusses marriage and assigns different conventions to different social groups, and it reserves some situations for particular classes of people. Readers should not treat the idealised world of the conventions as a description of early Tamil society, and recent scholarship has emphasised the ways in which these conventions represent women’s voices through male authorship (Zvelebil 1992; Takahashi 1995).

docs.title: 10.6.1 The landscapes of love (tiṇai)
docs.text:
Love poetry is organised by tiṇai, “situations” or “landscapes”. Five of them are the core of the system; each pairs a phase of love with a landscape, a season and time of day, and a characteristic flower, from which it takes its name. The Tolkāppiyam adds two further tiṇais, kaikkiḷai (one-sided love) and peruntiṇai (mismatched or improper love), making seven (Table 10.6).

Table 10.6. The five principal akam tiṇais Tiṇai Landscape Phase of love Time kuṟiñci mountains union of lovers midnight; cold season mullai forest, pasture patient waiting evening; rainy season marutam riverine farmland sulking, quarrels over infidelity dawn neytal seashore anxious longing sunset pālai parched wasteland separation, elopement midday; summer

Each landscape has its “native elements” (karupporuḷ): gods, people, animals, birds, plants, occupations and music. A poem need not state its emotion: the mention of, say, a flower or a bird of a particular landscape is enough to evoke the situation. The Tolkāppiyam also discusses uḷḷuṟai, implied comparison through such natural details, and iṟaicci, suggestion. These ideas have been compared with the theory of suggestion (dhvani) developed later in Sanskrit poetics; the comparison is illuminating, but there is no evidence of direct influence in either direction (Figure 10.2).

Figure 10.2. The five principal tiṇais of Tamil love poetry

docs.title: 10.6.2 The poetry of the exterior (puṟam)
docs.text:
The Tolkāppiyam classifies heroic poetry into seven puṟam tiṇais, each paired with one of the seven akam tiṇais. A later treatise, the Puṟapporuḷ Veṇpāmālai, has a different and larger scheme, in which the defence of cattle (karantai) and the defence of a fort (nocci) appear as separate themes (Table 10.7).

Table 10.7. The seven puṟam tiṇais of the Tolkāppiyam and their akam counterparts Puṟam tiṇai Theme Paired with veṭci cattle raid kuṟiñci vañci invasion, the march to war mullai uḻiñai siege of a fort marutam tumpai pitched battle neytal vākai victory pālai kāñci the transience of life peruntiṇai pāṭāṇ praise of a patron kaikkiḷai

docs.title: 10.7 Tamil Prosody (yāppu)
docs.text:
The Poruḷatikāram includes a chapter on prosody (Ceyyuḷiyal), and later treatises such as the Yāpparuṅkalam and its abridgement, the Yāpparuṅkalakkārikai, developed the subject. Tamil prosody is independent of Sanskrit metre. Its basic unit is the acai, a group of one or two syllables of a particular weight (nēr or nirai); acais combine to form the metrical foot (cīr), feet form the line (aṭi), and the links between feet are governed by rules of connection (taḷai). Ornamentation by alliteration of initial sounds (mōṉai) and by second-syllable rhyme (etukai), collectively toṭai, is an essential feature.

The classical verse forms include the āciriyappā (akaval), the flexible metre of most Caṅkam poetry; the veṇpā, a strict and concise form, used for example in the couplets of the Tirukkuṟaḷ; the kalippā, associated with dramatic and dialogue poems; and the vañcippā. Kannada and Telugu developed prosodic systems that combine Sanskrit metres with indigenous Dravidian forms, such as the Kannada ṣaṭpadi and the Telugu dvipada.

docs.title: 10.8 Tamil and Sanskrit in the Tolkāppiyam
docs.text:
Tamil and Sanskrit have been in contact for more than two thousand years. The Tolkāppiyam itself has rules for adapting Sanskrit words (vaṭacol, “northern words”) to Tamil sounds, and Caṅkam poetry already contains Sanskrit and Prakrit loanwords. The first couplet of the Tirukkuṟaḷ, a collection of aphorisms probably of the mid-1st millennium CE, quoted at the head of this chapter, shows both the Tamil theory of letters and the adaptation of Sanskrit words. It opens with the first letter, a, as the Tolkāppiyam orders them, and it is in the strict kuṟaḷ veṇpā form of four feet followed by three. Its words āti and pakavaṉ are Sanskrit ādi “first” and bhagavān “lord”, reshaped to fit Tamil phonology, which has no separate letters for voiced or aspirated stops.

The relationship grew closer in the medieval period, when Tamil grammarians began to describe their language through Sanskrit categories and some argued that Tamil grammar depended on Sanskrit, while others insisted on its independence. That debate, and its modern sequel in the discovery of the Dravidian family, the Tamil revival and the politics of language, are followed in Chapter 11. Both the debt of Tamil to Sanskrit and the debt of Sanskrit to the Dravidian languages are real, and modern scholarship tries to describe them without the polemics of either side (Krishnamurti 2003).

docs.title: 10.9 The Living Tradition
docs.text: The Tolkāppiyam holds a special place in modern Tamil culture as a symbol of the antiquity and independence of Tamil. In the 20th century the Tamil revival movement, and the politics of language in Tamil Nadu, gave it renewed public prominence (Ramaswamy 1997). In 2004 Tamil became the first language to be declared a “classical language” by the Government of India.

docs.title: Chapter 11: After the Tolkāppiyam: Grammars of Tamil, Kannada, Telugu and Malayalam
docs.text:
dēśabhāṣalanduṁ deluṁgu lessa Among the languages of the land, Telugu is the finest.

— the god to the king in a dream, in Kṛṣṇadevarāya’s Āmuktamālyada 1.15 (early 16th century)

docs.title: 11.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The Tolkāppiyam (Chapter 10) stood alone for many centuries. From the 9th century onwards, however, each of the four literary Dravidian languages acquired grammars of its own, and these works form one of the largest bodies of grammatical writing in India outside Sanskrit (Table 11.1). They are usually passed over in a sentence. This chapter looks inside them: how they are organised, what categories they use, how they handle the Sanskrit vocabulary that flowed into every southern language, what they reveal about the languages of their time, and how their classifications led to the modern discovery of the Dravidian family.

Table 11.1. The main Dravidian grammars after the Tolkāppiyam (dates approximate) Language Work Author Date; written in Tamil Iṟaiyaṉār Akapporuḷ attributed to Iṟaiyaṉār commentary c. 8th c.; Tamil Tamil Vīracōḻiyam Puttamittiraṉ 11th c.; Tamil Tamil Naṉṉūl Pavaṇanti early 13th c.; Tamil Tamil Ilakkaṇa Viḷakkam Vaittiyanāta Tēcikar 17th c.; Tamil Kannada Kavirājamārga Śrīvijaya (or Nṛpatuṅga) c. 850; Kannada Kannada Karṇāṭakabhāṣābhūṣaṇa Nāgavarma II 1140s; Sanskrit Kannada Śabdamaṇidarpaṇa Keśirāja c. 1260; Kannada Kannada Karṇāṭakaśabdānuśāsana Bhaṭṭākalaṅka 1604; Sanskrit Telugu Āndhraśabdacintāmaṇi attributed to Nannaya date disputed; Sanskrit Telugu Āndhrabhāṣābhūṣaṇamu Ketana 13th c.; Telugu Telugu Appakavīyamu Appakavi 1656; Telugu Telugu Bālavyākaraṇamu Paravastu Cinnaya Sūri 1858; Telugu Malayalam Līlātilakam anonymous late 14th c.; Sanskrit Malayalam Kēraḷapāṇinīyam A. R. Rājarāja Varma 1896; Malayalam

Three features recur. First, the language in which a grammar is written is itself a statement. Some grammars of Kannada and Telugu were composed in Sanskrit sūtras or verses, others in the language they describe, and the choice says something about the readership and about the status of the language. Second, every one of these traditions had to classify words by origin: native words, Sanskrit words taken over unchanged, Sanskrit words reshaped, and words from neighbouring languages. These classifications, a Dravidian development of an idea also found among the Prakrit grammarians (Chapter 9), turned out to be the starting point of the modern discovery of the Dravidian family. Third, the grammars belong to the process that Sheldon Pollock has called vernacularisation, in which regional languages became languages of literature and courtly culture on the model of Sanskrit (Section 1.6). Grammar was one of the things a literary language had to possess, and a king who sponsored one claimed a share of the prestige that grammar had long conferred on Sanskrit (Pollock 2006).

docs.title: 11.2 The Tamil Tradition after the Tolkāppiyam
11.2.1 Between the Tolkāppiyam and the Vīracōḻiyam
docs.text: The Iṟaiyaṉār Akapporuḷ, a short treatise on the poetics of love ascribed to Iṟaiyaṉār, a name of Śiva, is known together with a prose commentary traditionally attributed to Nakkīrar (c. 8th century). The preface of this commentary is the source of the legend of three successive literary academies (caṅkam) at Madurai, the first two lasting thousands of years and losing their works to the sea; historians treat the legend as a later construction, though it gave the Caṅkam poems their name. In the 10th century the Jain Amitacākarar’s Yāpparuṅkalam and its abridgement, the Yāpparuṅkalakkārikai, became the standard works on prosody (Section 10.7).

docs.title: 11.2.2 The Vīracōḻiyam and the five divisions
docs.text:
The first major Tamil grammar after the Tolkāppiyam was written by a Buddhist, Puttamittiraṉ (Buddhamitra), a local chief who named it after his overlord, the Cōḻa king Vīrarājendra (r. 1063–1070). The Vīracōḻiyam is composed in the kalitturai verse form and was explained by a commentary of Peruntēvaṉār. It is remarkable for two reasons. It deliberately describes Tamil through the categories of Sanskrit grammar: its first section is called canti (Sanskrit sandhi) and it introduces the Sanskrit kāraka relations and secondary derivatives (taddhita) into Tamil grammar. And it treats grammar in five divisions instead of the Tolkāppiyam’s three: letters (eḻuttu), words (col), subject-matter (poruḷ), prosody (yāppu) and figures of speech (aṇi). The last of these was adapted from Daṇḍin’s Kāvyādarśa, which had also been rendered into Tamil as the Taṇṭiyalaṅkāram, probably in the 12th century (Zvelebil 1995).

The scheme of five divisions (aintilakkaṇam) became standard. When later Tamil scholars spoke of “grammar” (ilakkaṇam), they meant this whole field of letters, words, poetic subject-matter, metre and ornament. The scope was far wider than Sanskrit vyākaraṇa, which left metre and poetics to separate sciences (Chapters 3 and 8). The Tamil grammarian was by definition also a theorist of literature.

docs.title: 11.2.3 The Naṉṉūl
docs.text:
The Naṉṉūl (“The Good Book”) of the Jain scholar Pavaṇanti, written in the early 13th century under the patronage of a Gaṅga chief named Cīyagaṅkaṉ, is the most successful grammar in the history of Tamil. It covers only the first two divisions, letters and words, in some 460 short verse rules (nūṟpā), arranged in two books of five chapters each. Its success came from its clarity. Where the Tolkāppiyam is archaic, allusive and in places obscure, the Naṉṉūl is systematic, and it describes the Tamil of the medieval literary language rather than that of the Caṅkam age. For seven centuries it was the grammar that Tamil students learned by heart, and it was still the basis of school grammar in the 19th century (Zvelebil 1995).

The work opens with a long general preface (potuppāyiram) that is a small treatise on scholarship. It defines what a proper treatise (nūl) is, lists the faults a treatise must avoid and the “devices” (utti) by which it expounds its subject, and describes the qualities of a good teacher and a good student and the right manner of teaching and learning. The list of thirty-two devices, which the Tolkāppiyam also gives, is the Tamil counterpart of the Sanskrit tantrayukti, the methods of scientific exposition listed in the Arthaśāstra and the medical classics. The preface’s grading of students, in which the best are compared to the swan that separates milk from water, has been quoted in Tamil schools ever since.

The Naṉṉūl also refines the Tolkāppiyam’s analysis of sounds. It keeps the thirty primary letters, twelve vowels and eighteen consonants, but recognises ten dependent letters (cārpeḻuttu) instead of three. Besides the āytam and the shortened i and u, it counts the consonant–vowel syllable (uyirmey), the prolonged vowels and consonants used in verse (aḷapeṭai), and the shortened forms of ai, au, m and the āytam that occur in particular positions. These are not new sounds. They are positional variants, and the Naṉṉūl’s willingness to list them is a sign of its interest in exact description of the spoken and recited language.

docs.title: 11.2.4 Analysing the word
docs.text:
The Naṉṉūl’s most influential contribution is its analysis of the inflected word. It divides words into those that can be analysed into parts (pakupatam) and those that cannot (pakāpatam), and it names up to six components of an analysable word: the base (pakuti, from Sanskrit prakṛti); the final suffix (vikuti, from Sanskrit vikṛti), which marks person, number and gender; the “middle element” (iṭainilai), typically the tense marker; a linking sound (canti); an empty augment (cāriyai), which carries no meaning; and the change (vikāram) that any of these may undergo. The standard school illustration is naṭantāṉ, “he walked” (Figure 11.1).

Figure 11.1. The Naṉṉūl’s analysis of an inflected Tamil word, in the usual school illustration

The Sanskrit terms prakṛti and vikṛti were borrowed. The analysis they serve is a Tamil one, built for an agglutinative language in which a stem is followed by a string of separable suffixes (Section 10.5). It is comparable, in its own terms, to the morphological segmentation that modern descriptive grammars of Tamil use.

Like the Tolkāppiyam before it, the Naṉṉūl classifies the vocabulary of poetry into four kinds: ordinary native words (iyaṟcol), literary or modified words (tiricol), words from neighbouring regions (ticaiccol) and “northern words” (vaṭacol), that is, Sanskrit. It adds rules for the treatment of Sanskrit words. Those that contain only sounds common to both languages can enter Tamil unchanged; those containing sounds peculiar to Sanskrit must be reshaped, so that, for example, voiced and aspirated stops are replaced by the corresponding Tamil letters. This is the same procedure seen in the first couplet of the Tirukkuṟaḷ (Section 10.8).

docs.title: 11.2.5 Commentators, compendia and the quarrel over Sanskrit
docs.text:
The Naṉṉūl attracted a long line of commentators. Mayilainātar (perhaps 14th century) wrote the oldest surviving commentary. Caṅkaranamaccivāyar’s commentary, written in the 17th or early 18th century and revised by Civañāṉa Muṉivar, became the standard school text. In the 19th century Āṟumuka Nāvalar of Jaffna edited it for the new printed school books. Alongside the commentaries stood comprehensive compendia that again covered all five divisions. The most important is the Ilakkaṇa Viḷakkam of Vaittiyanāta Tēcikar of Tiruvārūr (17th century), nicknamed the “little Tolkāppiyam”. Another is the Toṉṉūl Viḷakkam of the Jesuit Beschi (Vīramāmuṉivar), who also wrote Latin grammars of literary and colloquial Tamil for missionaries in the 1720s and 1730s (Zvelebil 1992).

Medieval literary Tamil had in any case moved close to Sanskrit. The Vīracōḻiyam’s commentator had already suggested that Tamil grammar depended on Sanskrit, Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava commentators wrote in a Tamil heavily laden with Sanskrit, and in Kerala and parts of the Tamil country a mixed literary style, maṇipravāḷam, combined Sanskrit with Tamil or Malayalam freely (Section 11.6). The 17th and 18th centuries then saw an open argument about the relation of Tamil grammar to Sanskrit, more than a century before Caldwell. On one side, the Pirayōka Vivēkam of Cuppiramaṇiya Tīkṣitar (17th century) set out to show that the categories of Tamil grammar could be derived from those of Sanskrit, and the Ilakkaṇakkottu of Cāmināta Tēcikar (17th century) contains a frequently quoted dismissive remark, that a language with only five letters of its own hardly deserves a separate grammar. On the other, Civañāṉa Muṉivar (d. 1785), a Śaiva monk of the Tiruvāvaṭuturai monastery and an accomplished Sanskritist, answered in a long commentary on the preface and the first rule of the Tolkāppiyam, defending the independence of the Tamil grammatical tradition and the standing of Tamil as a language equal to Sanskrit. In keeping with Śaiva tradition, he held that Śiva had given Sanskrit grammar to Pāṇini and Tamil grammar to Agastya. The terms of this debate were theological and literary, not historical. Its significance is that the question later answered by comparative philology, whether Tamil is “of” Sanskrit, was already a live and contested question within the Tamil grammatical tradition itself.

docs.title: 11.3.1 The Kavirājamārga
docs.text: The earliest surviving Kannada literary work is not a poem but a treatise on how poetry should be written in Kannada. The Kavirājamārga (“The Royal Road of Poets”), composed around 850 at the Rāṣṭrakūṭa court, is attributed to the king Nṛpatuṅga Amoghavarṣa I or, more probably, to a court poet, Śrīvijaya. Its poetics follow Daṇḍin, and its literary side is discussed in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā. What concerns us here is its awareness of language. It defines the Kannada country as the land between the Kāverī and the Godāvarī. It names the area around Kisuvoḷal (Paṭṭadakal), Kopaṇa (Koppaḷ), Puligere (Lakṣmeśvara) and Oṅkunda as the home of the purest Kannada. It notes that usage varies from region to region. And it warns poets against incongruous mixtures of Sanskrit and Kannada. Pollock has read the work as a founding document of a regional literary culture. Kannada is presented as a language with a defined territory, a standard and a correct literary form, and so as a fit vehicle for courtly literature beside Sanskrit (Pollock 2006).

docs.title: 11.3.2 Nāgavarma II
docs.text: Kannada grammar proper begins with Nāgavarma II, a Jain scholar who was instructor to the army (kaṭakopādhyāya) at the court of the Western Cāḷukya king Jagadekamalla II in the 1140s. He wrote on Kannada in both languages. His Kāvyāvalokana, in Kannada verse, is a treatise on poetics whose first part, the Śabdasmṛti, is a grammar of Kannada; his Karṇāṭakabhāṣābhūṣaṇa is a grammar of Kannada in Sanskrit sūtras with a Sanskrit commentary; and he also compiled a lexicon of the vocabulary of poetry, the Abhidhānavastukośa. The same author thus addressed two audiences: Kannada poets, and scholars trained in Sanskrit who expected a grammar to look like one of their own.

docs.title: 11.3.3 Keśirāja’s Śabdamaṇidarpaṇa
docs.text:
The classic grammar of Old Kannada is the Śabdamaṇidarpaṇa (“Jewel-Mirror of Words”) of Keśirāja, written in the Hoysaḷa period around 1260. Unlike Nāgavarma’s Sanskrit grammar, it is written in Kannada, in the kanda metre, with the author’s own prose commentary. Its order broadly follows the Sanskrit grammars of its day, moving from letters and their combination (sandhi) through nouns, compounds and secondary derivatives to verbs and verbal roots, words derived from Sanskrit and Prakrit, and indeclinables. What it describes, however, is Kannada as found in the works of the great poets. Keśirāja states rules and then illustrates them with lines from Pampa, Ponna, Ranna and other earlier poets, whose usage he treats as the authority for correct Kannada. This makes the grammar an anthology of the classical literature as well as a description of it.

The Śabdamaṇidarpaṇa is also a precious historical record. Old Kannada still had two sounds that later disappeared: the alveolar ṟ and the retroflex approximant ḻ, each with a letter of its own in the Kannada script, both inherited from Proto-Dravidian and both still present in Tamil and Malayalam. Keśirāja gives rules and word-lists for their correct use, which is valuable evidence for historians of the language. In later Kannada ṟ merged with r and ḻ with ḷ. He is also strict about compounds. A compound should not join a Sanskrit word to a Kannada one except under defined conditions, and the Kannada tradition calls such a faulty mixed compound arisamāsa (“enemy compound”).

docs.title: 11.3.4 Bhaṭṭākalaṅka
docs.text: The last great traditional grammar of Kannada returned to Sanskrit. Bhaṭṭākalaṅka’s Karṇāṭakaśabdānuśāsana (1604), by a Jain scholar, describes Kannada in nearly six hundred Sanskrit sūtras on the Pāṇinian model, with two layers of the author’s own commentary. Its very form was an argument: Kannada, it implied, deserved a grammar as rigorous as Sanskrit’s and could be described in the same scientific language. The modern study of Kannada was founded in the late 19th century by Ferdinand Kittel of the Basel Mission. His Kannada–English Dictionary (1894), compiled with the help of Indian scholars, drew systematically on the old grammars and lexicons.

docs.title: 11.4.1 The Āndhraśabdacintāmaṇi and its date
docs.text:
Telugu tradition begins its grammatical history with Nannaya, the 11th-century poet who began the Telugu Mahābhārata at the Eastern Cāḷukya court of Rājarāja Narendra at Rājamahendravaram. To him is attributed the Āndhraśabdacintāmaṇi, a short grammar of Telugu in Sanskrit verses in the āryā metre. Its five sections, on technical terms (saṃjñā), combination (sandhi), stems ending in vowels (ajanta), stems ending in consonants (halanta) and the verb (kriyā), follow the plan of a Sanskrit grammar. It treats Telugu as a language derived from Sanskrit and Prakrit, so that much of its work consists in stating how Sanskrit words take Telugu form.

The attribution to Nannaya is traditional and much doubted. The work is not mentioned by the 13th-century grammarian Ketana, who claims to be the first to write a grammar of Telugu in Telugu, and its earliest known commentaries are centuries later than Nannaya. Many modern scholars therefore place it well after the 11th century, though no date has been established. Whatever its date, it was accepted from the 17th century onwards as the foundational grammar of Telugu, and its authority was bound up with Nannaya’s status as the “first poet” (ādikavi) of Telugu literature (Narayana Rao 2003).

docs.title: 11.4.2 Ketana and the first grammar in Telugu
docs.text: Mūlaghaṭika Ketana, a 13th-century poet who dedicated a Telugu version of Daṇḍin’s Daśakumāracarita to the great Mahābhārata poet Tikkana, wrote the Āndhrabhāṣābhūṣaṇamu (“Ornament of the Telugu Language”). It is a short grammar of about two hundred Telugu verses. Its importance lies less in its detail than in its choice of language. Ketana addressed Telugu poets in Telugu, and he gave an early statement of the classification of Telugu vocabulary that later grammarians developed (Section 11.5). Other early works are attributed to a grammarian named Atharvaṇa, among them a treatise on the derivation of tadbhava words (Vikṛtiviveka); their date and authorship are uncertain.

docs.title: 11.4.3 Appakavi, the commentators and Cinnaya Sūri
docs.text:
In 1656 Kākunūri Appakavi composed the Appakavīyamu, a long Telugu verse treatise on grammar and prosody, presented as an exposition of the Āndhraśabdacintāmaṇi. Appakavi tells a story of how Nannaya’s grammar had been lost and was recovered, and his work did much to establish its authority. A Sanskrit commentary on the Āndhraśabdacintāmaṇi by Ahobala became the other standard aid to its study.

The tradition culminated in Paravastu Cinnaya Sūri’s Bālavyākaraṇamu (1858), written in Telugu sūtras on the Pāṇinian pattern with great concision. Cinnaya Sūri worked as a teacher of Telugu in Madras, where Telugu grammar had been studied by Indian and British scholars at the College of Fort St. George since the early 19th century. His grammar fixed the norms of the literary language (grāndhika) so firmly that the 20th-century campaign for the spoken standard, described below, was largely a campaign against it. The colonial grammars and dictionaries of Telugu stood beside it. They include A. D. Campbell’s Grammar of the Teloogoo Language (1816) and C. P. Brown’s grammar (1840) and Dictionary, Telugu and English (1852). Lisa Mitchell has shown how in the 19th and 20th centuries these works, together with print and schooling, helped turn Telugu from one of several languages of a multilingual region into the object of an intense “mother tongue” devotion (Mitchell 2009).

These grammars described the literary language, and in each region the distance between that language and everyday speech grew over the centuries. In the early 20th century the question became a public controversy. In Telugu, the scholar Gidugu Venkata Ramamurti campaigned for the use of the spoken standard (vyāvahārika) in prose and in schools, against the defenders of the classical literary language codified by Cinnaya Sūri; the spoken standard eventually prevailed in prose, journalism and education. Similar tensions between a classical written norm and the modern spoken language shaped the standardisation of Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam, a modern counterpart of the old relationship between Sanskrit and the Prakrits (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 11.5 Words and Their Origins
docs.text:
Every literary Dravidian language absorbed a large vocabulary from Sanskrit and Prakrit, and every grammatical tradition developed a classification of words by origin. The categories differ in detail, but they share a common purpose, which is to decide which words a poet may use and in what form (Table 11.2).

Table 11.2. The classification of vocabulary by origin in four grammatical traditions (simplified) Tradition Native words Words from Sanskrit Other classes Prakrit grammarians (Chapter 9) deśī (“regional”) tatsama (identical), tadbhava (derived by sound change) — Tamil (Tolkāppiyam, Naṉṉūl) iyaṟcol (ordinary), tiricol (literary, modified) vaṭacol (“northern words”), unchanged or reshaped ticaiccol (words of neighbouring regions) Kannada (Keśirāja and later) deśya, deśī (pure Kannada) tatsama, tadbhava mixed compounds restricted (arisamāsa) Telugu (Ketana and later) deśya (pure Telugu) tatsama, tadbhava anyadeśya (from other languages); grāmya (colloquial, excluded from poetry)

In the Telugu scheme a tatsama is a Sanskrit (or Prakrit) word used with Telugu endings, as in rāmuḍu for Sanskrit rāma. A tadbhava is one reshaped according to Telugu sound patterns. The deśya words are the native core, which the grammarians recognised could not be derived from Sanskrit at all. The category of grāmya, the rustic or colloquial, marks the boundary between the literary language and everyday speech. It was this boundary that the reformers of the early 20th century set out to remove.

These classifications were descriptive tools in the service of literary correctness, not theories of language history. The Telugu grammarians in particular assumed that Telugu was in some sense a transformation of Sanskrit. Yet by setting apart a large body of native words that could not be traced to Sanskrit, they isolated exactly the evidence that a historical linguist would need. As Section 11.7 shows, this is how the comparative case for a Dravidian family was first made.

docs.title: 11.6 Malayalam: The Līlātilakam and After
docs.text:
The Līlātilakam, an anonymous Sanskrit treatise of the late 14th century, is the earliest work to describe the language of Kerala. It is written as sūtras with a prose commentary, in eight sections (śilpa), and combines grammar with poetics. Its subject is maṇipravāḷam, the literary style of Kerala that mixed Malayalam and Sanskrit, which it defines in its opening rule as the union of the “language” (bhāṣā) and Sanskrit. The name compares the mixture to a string of rubies and coral beads, two red stones that should blend without visible seams. The text asks which Sanskrit words may enter such verse, when they may keep their Sanskrit case endings and when they must take Malayalam ones, and which combinations are graceful and which are faults. It also distinguishes maṇipravāḷam from pāṭṭu, the song tradition composed in Dravidian letters and metres with the rhyme and alliteration of Tamil verse. In discussing the “language” it separates the speech of Kerala from the Tamil of the Pāṇḍya and Cōḻa countries. It is thus one of the earliest explicit statements that Malayalam was becoming a language distinct from Tamil (Freeman 1998). Malayalam had developed from the western dialects of the Tamil-speaking region, and it emerged as a distinct literary language in the late medieval period. From the 16th century the devotional poet Tuñcattu Eḻuttacchaṉ, who wrote extensively in a style rich in Sanskrit vocabulary and in the Grantha-derived script, was regarded as a father of literary Malayalam.

The modern grammatical study of Malayalam began with the Basel missionary Hermann Gundert. He published a Malayalam grammar (1851, enlarged 1868) and a Malayalam and English Dictionary (1872) that remains a standard historical source. It culminated in A. R. Rājarāja Varma’s Kēraḷapāṇinīyam (1896; revised 1917). As its title suggests, Rājarāja Varma set out to do for Malayalam what Pāṇini had done for Sanskrit, but he also asked a historical question: how had Malayalam become different from Tamil? His answer was a list of six changes (naya) that, he argued, separated the two languages. The best known are the loss of personal endings on the verb (puruṣabhedanirāsam), so that Malayalam avan vannu “he came” and ñān vannu “I came” share one verb form where Tamil distinguishes vantāṉ and vantēṉ, and the assimilation of nasal clusters (anunāsikātiprasaram), so that Malayalam vannu corresponds to Tamil vantu “having come”. The Kēraḷapāṇinīyam thus combined the traditional form of a Pāṇinian grammar with the comparative method of Caldwell, and it shows how quickly Indian grammarians made the new historical linguistics their own.

docs.title: 11.7 The Dravidian Family: Before and After Caldwell
docs.text: Indian scholars had long known that Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam differed in vocabulary and structure from Sanskrit, and the grammarians’ classifications of vocabulary had isolated their native core. The demonstration that they form a separate language family was made in Madras in 1816 by Francis Whyte Ellis, working with Indian scholars of the College of Fort St. George; Robert Caldwell gave the family its name and its first systematic description in 1856; and modern comparative work, above all T. Burrow and M. B. Emeneau’s Dravidian Etymological Dictionary and the synthesis of Bhadriraju Krishnamurti, has confirmed and refined the result (Burrow and Emeneau 1984; Krishnamurti 2003). The arguments themselves, and the use that was made of them, deserve a closer look.

docs.title: 11.7.1 Ellis and the Indian grammarians
docs.text: Ellis’s demonstration appeared as a “Note to the Introduction” in A. D. Campbell’s Grammar of the Teloogoo Language (Madras, 1816). Campbell, following the Telugu grammarians, had presented Telugu as derived from Sanskrit. Ellis argued the opposite. He took the native (deśya) roots of Telugu, set them beside the corresponding roots of Tamil and Kannada, and showed that the three languages shared a large stock of basic roots that had no Sanskrit source. The Sanskrit element, however large, was borrowed, while the native core was common inheritance. Thomas Trautmann has shown that this argument rested on Indian scholarship. Its raw materials were the Telugu grammarians’ own distinction of deśya from tatsama and tadbhava, and lists of Telugu roots prepared by learned Indian staff of the College of Fort St. George, among them Paṭṭābhirāma Śāstri. The “Dravidian proof”, in Trautmann’s phrase, was a collaborative product of colonial Madras, not a European discovery imposed on India (Trautmann 2006).

docs.title: 11.7.2 Caldwell’s arguments
docs.text:
Robert Caldwell (1814–1891), a missionary in the Tirunelveli district, published his Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian or South-Indian Family of Languages in 1856 and a much enlarged second edition in 1875 (Caldwell 1856). He took the name “Dravidian” from the Sanskrit drāviḍa, noting its use by the Mīmāṃsaka Kumārila Bhaṭṭa (7th century), who refers to an “Āndhra–Drāviḍa language”. His case rested on grammatical structure as well as vocabulary: on the shared personal pronouns and numerals, among the most stable parts of any language; on agglutinative suffixation, as against the fusional inflection of Sanskrit; on the negative conjugation of the verb; on the division of nouns into rational and irrational classes, the Tamil uyartiṇai and aḵṟiṇai (Section 10.5); and on the absence of Sanskrit-type prefixes and of grammatical gender based on form. He argued that Tamil, in particular, could dispense with its Sanskrit vocabulary altogether. He also suggested that influence had run the other way, and that the retroflex consonants of Sanskrit owed something to Dravidian contact, a suggestion that later work on the South Asian linguistic area has broadly supported (Section 1.8).

Not all of Caldwell’s views have lasted. His proposed relationship between Dravidian and the “Scythian” (Ural-Altaic) languages has not been accepted. Later long-range proposals, such as a link with Elamite, also remain unproven (Krishnamurti 2003). His book also carried the racial and religious assumptions of its time. It portrayed the Brahmins as Aryan immigrants who had brought higher civilisation to the south. His earlier tract on the Shanar (Nadar) community of Tirunelveli, written from a missionary standpoint, was deeply resented by the community it described.

docs.title: 11.7.3 The family today
docs.text:
Krishnamurti counts about twenty-six Dravidian languages in four subgroups (Table 11.3). Many of the smaller ones are spoken by Adivasi communities in central and eastern India, and Brahui is spoken in Balochistan, far to the north-west. Shared features of the family include agglutinative morphology, verb-final word order, postpositions, a distinction between inclusive and exclusive “we”, participial constructions in place of relative pronouns, negative verb forms and the semantic gender system already described in the Tolkāppiyam, which as the earliest systematic description of a Dravidian language remains an important source for the reconstruction of Proto-Dravidian (Krishnamurti 2003; Steever 1998).

Table 11.3. The subgroups of the Dravidian family, following Krishnamurti (2003) Subgroup Languages South Dravidian I Tamil, Malayalam, Iruḷa, Kota, Toda, Badaga, Kannada, Kodagu, Tulu South Dravidian II (South-Central) Telugu, Gondi, Konda, Kui, Kuvi, Pengo, Manda Central Dravidian Kolami, Naiki, Parji, Ollari, Gadaba North Dravidian Kurux, Malto, Brahui

docs.title: 11.7.4 Afterlives
docs.text: The linguistic result was sound and has been confirmed by every later study. Its social reading was another matter. In the late 19th and 20th centuries “Dravidian” became the name of a political and cultural identity in Tamil Nadu, opposed to “Aryan” Brahmin and Sanskritic culture, and Caldwell’s demonstration was cited as scientific proof of the independence and antiquity of Tamil. In 1916 Maṟaimalai Aṭikaḷ launched the “pure Tamil” movement (taṉittamiḻ iyakkam), which sought to replace Sanskrit loanwords with Tamil ones, and language became bound up with the Dravidian political movement and with opposition to Hindi (Ramaswamy 1997). In its extreme form this produced claims that Tamil was the original language of humanity. The best-known proponent was the scholar Ñā. Tēvanēyaṉ (Dēvanēyap Pāvāṇar), who tied this view to the legend of a lost southern continent. The claim mirrors the belief that Sanskrit is the mother of all languages and has no more support (Section 14.13). Modern comparative Dravidian treats Dravidian as one ancient family among the several of South Asia, with a long history of mutual borrowing with Indo-Aryan, neither its parent nor its offspring (Burrow and Emeneau 1984; Krishnamurti 2003).

docs.title: 11.8 Assessment
docs.text: Measured against Pāṇini, the medieval grammars of the Dravidian languages can look derivative: many borrow Sanskrit terms, several are written in Sanskrit, and the Telugu tradition long described its language as a transformation of Sanskrit. Measured on their own terms, they are a considerable achievement. They gave four languages written norms that sustained their literatures for centuries. They described sounds and forms, such as the Kannada ṟ and ḻ or the Tamil positional variants, that would otherwise be known only from manuscripts. And they built a classification of vocabulary that made the modern discovery of the Dravidian family possible. Their history also shows that the relation of the southern languages to Sanskrit was debated by Indian grammarians long before it became a question of colonial science and modern politics.
