docs.title: Chapter 12: Writing and Scripts: From the Indus Seals to Devanāgarī
docs.text:
liper yathāvadgrahaṇena vāṅmayaṃ nadīmukheneva samudram āviśat By learning the script properly he entered the ocean of literature, as one enters the sea by the mouth of a river.

— Kālidāsa, Raghuvaṃśa 3.28, of the young prince Raghu

docs.title: 12.1 Introduction: Writing in an Oral Culture
docs.text: The traditions described in the earlier chapters of this volume were developed and transmitted largely by word of mouth. The Vedas were memorised, Pāṇini’s rules were learned by heart, and even after writing became common, learning “from a book” was considered inferior to learning from a teacher. Yet South Asia also has one of the world’s richest histories of writing. The Indus civilisation used a script that remains undeciphered; from the 3rd century BCE the Brāhmī and Kharoṣṭhī scripts appear in the inscriptions of Aśoka; and Brāhmī became the ancestor of scores of scripts used today across South, Southeast and Central Asia. Perso-Arabic scripts, used in Sindh from the 8th century and across much of northern India from the 11th–12th, form a second great family of writing in the subcontinent (Salomon 1998; Falk 1993).

docs.title: 12.2 The Indus Script
docs.text:
The earliest writing in South Asia is found on objects of the mature Indus (Harappan) civilisation, c. 2600–1900 BCE: stamp seals, sealings, tablets, pottery and a few other objects, of which some 4,000 or more inscribed examples are known. Estimates of the number of distinct signs range from about 400 to about 700, depending on how variants are counted (Mahadevan 1977; Parpola 1994). The inscriptions are very short, typically about five signs, and even the longest has fewer than thirty. They were usually written from right to left, as the spacing and cramping of signs at the left end of inscriptions shows, and the number of signs suggests a logo-syllabic system that, like other early scripts, combined word-signs with signs for sounds. The language or languages written are unknown. Proposals include an early form of Dravidian, argued at length by Asko Parpola and Iravatham Mahadevan, Indo-Aryan, Munda and lost languages of other families (Figure 12.1).

Figure 12.1. Indus objects in a museum display: at the right, a large square tablet (possibly an enlarged replica of a seal) carved with an elephant beneath a short inscription in the undeciphered Indus script; at the left, a small seal Photo: Royroydeb, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

No proposed decipherment has won general acceptance, and none can be tested without longer texts or a bilingual inscription. Steve Farmer, Richard Sproat and Michael Witzel argued in 2004 that the Indus signs did not encode language at all but were a system of non-linguistic symbols; other scholars have rejected this argument on statistical and archaeological grounds (Farmer et al. 2004). Rajesh Rao and his colleagues, for example, found that the sequences of Indus signs show a degree of order, measured as conditional entropy, close to that of known writing systems and unlike that of non-linguistic sign systems (Rao et al. 2009); the significance of such measures has itself been disputed. The question remains open. Claims that the Indus script has been read as Sanskrit, or as any other known language, and claims that Brāhmī descends from it, should be treated with great caution: there is a gap of more than a thousand years between the end of the Indus script and the first Brāhmī inscriptions, and no intermediate stages have been found (Figure 12.2).

Figure 12.2. A nineteenth-century drawing of a Harappan seal (a bull with an inscription), with an early attempt to read the signs as Brāhmī letters (“Lachhmiya”). Such readings have not been accepted Drawing: Alexander Cunningham, from Inscriptions of Asoka (1877), plate XXVIII, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 12.3 Brāhmī
docs.text: Brāhmī is the ancestor of almost all the indigenous scripts of South and Southeast Asia and of the Tibetan script. Its earliest securely dated examples are the inscriptions of Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE), found across the subcontinent.

docs.title: 12.3.1 Characteristics
docs.text:
Brāhmī is an abugida or “alphasyllabary” (Section 12.6): each consonant sign includes an inherent vowel a, other vowels following a consonant are shown by marks attached to it, and vowels at the beginning of a syllable have separate signs. It is written from left to right, though a few very early examples run right to left. Aśokan Brāhmī already distinguishes aspirated from unaspirated and retroflex from dental consonants, the distinctions that matter in Indo-Aryan phonology, and has signs for the long vowels, but it does not yet write consonant clusters consistently.

The Aśokan scribes wrote with a certain economy. Double consonants, which were very frequent in the Prakrits, are usually written as single ones, and a nasal before another consonant is generally written with the anusvāra dot; vowel length is often marked inconsistently. A reader therefore had to know the language to read the text correctly, much as a reader of unvowelled Arabic or Hebrew does. Over the following centuries the system was refined: conjunct signs for consonant clusters were developed, especially once the script was used for Sanskrit, with its many clusters, and the regional forms of the letters began to diverge (Salomon 1998).

docs.title: 12.3.2 The origin of Brāhmī
docs.text:
Where Brāhmī came from is one of the most debated questions in Indian epigraphy (Salomon 1998; Falk 1993).

Semitic derivation The majority view among epigraphists, set out in detail by Georg Bühler in the 1890s and defended in modified form by Richard Salomon and Harry Falk, is that the basic shapes of many Brāhmī consonant signs were adapted from a Semitic script, most probably Aramaic, the administrative script of the Achaemenid Persian empire, which ruled the north-west of the subcontinent in the 6th–4th centuries BCE. The principle of the inherent vowel and of vowel marks, the systematic distinctions of aspiration and retroflexion, and the left-to-right direction would then be Indian innovations, made by people familiar with Indian phonetic analysis. Kharoṣṭhī, which clearly derives from Aramaic, provides a parallel. Indigenous origin Other scholars have argued that Brāhmī was an independent Indian creation, pointing to its systematic phonetic design and to the weakness of some of the proposed letter-by-letter correspondences with Semitic prototypes. A derivation from the Indus script was proposed in the 19th century and is still sometimes advanced, but the chronological gap and the absence of intermediate forms tell against it.

A related debate concerns the date of the script’s creation. Falk argued that Brāhmī was created in the early Maurya period, perhaps for Aśoka’s own inscriptions, on the model of Kharoṣṭhī (Falk 1993). Others point to evidence for earlier writing: inscribed potsherds from Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka, dated by their archaeological context to about the 4th century BCE (Coningham et al. 1996); and inscribed sherds from Tamil Nadu (Kodumanal, Porunthal and other sites), for which the excavators, led by K. Rajan, have reported radiocarbon dates in the 5th century BCE. These reports have not been independently confirmed, and how far the dates of the layers apply to the inscriptions themselves remains disputed. Pāṇini’s grammar mentions writing (lipi), which suggests that some script was known in the north-west in his time, possibly an Aramaic one (Section 5.2.2).

docs.title: 12.3.3 Tamil-Brāhmī
docs.text: A distinctive variety of Brāhmī was used in the Tamil country, mainly for short inscriptions in caves (often Jain rock shelters), on pottery and on coins. It was adapted to Tamil phonology, with signs for the sounds ḻ, ḷ, ṟ and ṉ, and with different conventions for marking vowel-less consonants. Iravatham Mahadevan’s corpus placed most of these inscriptions between the 2nd century BCE and the 4th century CE (Mahadevan 2003); the more recent radiocarbon evidence mentioned above has been read as pushing the beginnings earlier, but this remains debated. Tamil-Brāhmī is the ancestor of the Vaṭṭeḻuttu script. The modern Tamil script is usually derived from the southern script of the Pallava period, the parent also of Grantha, with some features carried over from the older Tamil tradition; the details are debated (Salomon 1998).

docs.title: 12.3.4 The Aśokan inscriptions
docs.text:
Aśoka’s inscriptions, the first large body of Indian writing, already show that the choice of script followed the region: Brāhmī over most of the subcontinent, Kharoṣṭhī in the north-west, and Greek and Aramaic at the western edge of the empire (Table 12.1).

Table 12.1. Some Aśokan inscriptions and their scripts Site Type Script Notes Girnar (Gujarat) Major Rock Edicts Brāhmī Language with western features Dhauli and Jaugada (Odisha) Major Rock Edicts Brāhmī Includes the “separate edicts” for Kaliṅga Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra (Pakistan) Major Rock Edicts Kharoṣṭhī North-western Prakrit Kandahar (Afghanistan) Rock inscriptions Greek and Aramaic Translations of Aśoka’s message for western subjects Sarnath Pillar Brāhmī The lion capital is the national emblem of India Nigali Sagar and Lumbini (Nepal) Pillars Brāhmī Record Aśoka’s visits to Buddhist sites

The decipherment of Aśokan Brāhmī by James Prinsep in 1837, building on the work of others, opened the history of ancient India to modern scholarship; until then the script had been unreadable for many centuries. Prinsep worked from bilingual coins of the Indo-Greek kings, with Greek on one side and Kharoṣṭhī or Brāhmī on the other, and from short donative inscriptions at Sanchi that all ended with the same two letters, which he correctly read as dānaṃ “gift”. Kharoṣṭhī was deciphered in the same years with the help of the bilingual coins. Indian epigraphy then grew into a discipline, with the work of Alexander Cunningham, Georg Bühler and J. F. Fleet, the founding of the journal Epigraphia Indica (1888), and the systematic survey of inscriptions by the Archaeological Survey of India and by Indian epigraphists such as D. C. Sircar (Salomon 1998).

docs.title: 12.4 Kharoṣṭhī
docs.text: Kharoṣṭhī was used in the north-west, in Gandhāra and neighbouring regions, from about the 3rd century BCE to the 3rd century CE, and in Central Asia, on documents from Niya and other sites, until the 4th century or later. It is written from right to left, like its Aramaic model. Like Brāhmī it marks vowels by signs attached to consonants, but it distinguishes long and short vowels poorly. It was the script of Gāndhārī Prakrit in inscriptions, on coins (often together with Greek), in administrative documents and in Buddhist manuscripts; the birch-bark scrolls found since the 1990s in Afghanistan and Pakistan are among the oldest Buddhist manuscripts in any language. Unlike Brāhmī, it left no descendants.

docs.title: 12.5 The Family of Brāhmī Scripts
docs.text:
From the early centuries CE Brāhmī diversified into regional styles, which by the late 1st millennium had become distinct scripts (Figure 12.3).

Figure 12.3. A simplified family tree of the Brāhmī scripts (after Salomon (1998)). Solid arrows mark descent, dashed arrows influence or a less direct line; each arrow stands for gradual development over centuries, and many intermediate and minor scripts are omitted

docs.title: 12.5.1 Devanāgarī
docs.text: Devanāgarī developed from the Nāgarī script of northern and western India, which took its characteristic form around the 8th–10th centuries. The name is usually explained as “(script) of the city of the gods”, but its origin is uncertain. It became the most widely used script for Sanskrit, and it is used today for Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, Konkani, Maithili, Dogri, Bodo and other languages. Its most visible feature is the headstroke (śirorekhā) that joins the letters of a word; its consonants, in the traditional phonetic order, are shown in Figure 2.2 (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 12.5.2 Other scripts of India
docs.text: Bengali–Assamese and Odia developed from the eastern script often called Gauḍī or Proto-Bengali; Tirhuta (Mithilākṣara), used for Maithili, belongs to the same branch. Gurmukhī used for Punjabi, especially in the Sikh scriptures, was standardised in the 16th century, traditionally by Guru Aṅgad, from scripts of the Śāradā–Laṇḍā family. Telugu and Kannada developed from the scripts of the Kadamba and Cāḷukya dynasties and remained a single script until about the 13th century. Grantha (“book” script) was used in the Tamil country to write Sanskrit, which the Tamil script could not represent fully; it influenced both the modern Tamil and the Malayalam scripts. Tamil has a small inventory of letters, matching Tamil phonology; it is written with the puḷḷi (dot) to mark a consonant without a vowel, a device already found in Tamil-Brāhmī. Regional and commercial scripts such as Modi (for Marathi), Kaithi (in northern India) and the Mahājanī scripts of merchants were widely used until the 20th century.

docs.title: 12.5.3 Perso-Arabic scripts
docs.text: From the 11th century, with the establishment of Persian-speaking rulers in northern India, the Arabic script, in its Persian form, became the script of administration and of a large literature in Persian. In the nastaʿlīq style it is used today for Urdu and Kashmiri; Sindhi uses a form of the Arabic script standardised in the 1850s; and Punjabi in Pakistan is written in the Perso-Arabic Shahmukhi script. The adaptation of the Arabic alphabet to Indo-Aryan required new letters, for example for the retroflex consonants and the aspirates. The Hindi–Urdu controversy of the 19th and 20th centuries was in large part a conflict over scripts, Devanāgarī against Perso-Arabic, with lasting political consequences (King 1994; Rai 2001).

docs.title: 12.5.4 New scripts
docs.text:
Several scripts have been created in modern times for languages with no script of their own or as a statement of identity. The best known is Ol Chiki, devised for Santali by Raghunath Murmu in the 1920s and now in official use; others include the Warang Citi script for Ho, and revived or reformed scripts such as Meetei Mayek for Manipuri. Many tribal and minority languages are written in Devanāgarī, Bengali, Odia or Latin script (Table 12.2).

Table 12.2. Major scripts in use in India today and some languages written in them Script Languages (selection) Devanāgarī Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, Konkani, Maithili, Dogri, Bodo, Sanskrit; also Santali, Sindhi and Kashmiri in some usage Bengali–Assamese Bengali, Assamese, Manipuri (alongside Meetei Mayek), Bishnupriya Gurmukhī Punjabi (in India) Gujarati Gujarati, Kutchi Odia Odia Telugu Telugu Kannada Kannada, Tulu, Konkani (in Karnataka), Kodava Malayalam Malayalam Tamil Tamil, Saurashtra (in some usage) Perso-Arabic (nastaʿlīq) Urdu, Kashmiri, Sindhi (Arabic-based Sindhi script) Ol Chiki Santali Meetei Mayek Manipuri (Meitei) Latin Mizo, Khasi, Garo, many Naga languages; Konkani in Goa (alongside Devanāgarī) Tibetan Ladakhi, Sikkimese and other Tibetic languages

docs.title: 12.6 The Abugida Principle
docs.text:
Brāhmī and its descendants represent a distinct type of writing system. The linguist Peter T. Daniels named it the abugida (from the first letters of the Ethiopic script, which works on the same principle) (Daniels and Bright 1996). In an abugida:

  1. each consonant sign carries an inherent vowel (a in Indian scripts);

  2. other vowels after a consonant are written by marks (mātrā) attached to it, above, below, before or after;

  3. a special mark (the virāma) cancels the inherent vowel;

  4. consonant clusters are written with combined forms (saṃyuktākṣara) or with the virāma. See Table 12.3.

Table 12.3. Types of writing system Type Examples Basic unit Vowels Alphabet Greek, Latin phoneme Separate letters for vowels and consonants Abjad Arabic, Hebrew consonant Vowels usually unwritten or marked optionally Abugida Brāhmī scripts, Ethiopic consonant with inherent vowel Marks attached to consonants Syllabary Japanese kana syllable Each sign a whole syllable Logo-syllabic Chinese; probably the Indus script morpheme and syllable Mostly unmarked

The traditional order of the letters in all these scripts follows the phonetic analysis of the Śikṣā texts: vowels first, then the stops arranged by place and manner of articulation, then the semivowels, sibilants and h (Chapter 2). It is a lasting monument of ancient phonetics. Whether the original designers of Brāhmī applied phonetic theory directly, or the order was imposed on the script later, is not known.

docs.title: 12.7 Indian Scripts Beyond South Asia
docs.text: Brāhmī-derived scripts spread far beyond South Asia (Figure 12.3). South Indian scripts of the Pallava type were carried to Southeast Asia, where inscriptions in Old Khmer and Cham appear from the 5th–7th centuries and the Kawi script of Old Javanese, the ancestor of the Javanese and Balinese scripts, from the 8th. Mon and then Burmese writing derive from the same southern source, the Burmese inscriptions beginning in the 11th–12th centuries, and the Thai and Lao scripts were adapted from Old Khmer, the Thai script from the late 13th century. In the north, the Tibetan script was created in the 7th century from a northern Brāhmī script of the Siddhamātṛkā type, by tradition by Thon mi Sambhoṭa (Section 14.2.1), and Siddhamātṛkā itself travelled with Buddhism to China and Japan.

docs.title: 12.7.1 Central Asia
docs.text: Along the Silk Road, Indian scripts were adapted to languages of quite different families. Kharoṣṭhī was used for Gāndhārī administrative documents in the kingdom of Shanshan (around Niya, in the Tarim basin) in the 3rd–4th centuries. Brāhmī, in its northern “Central Asian” varieties, was used to write Sanskrit Buddhist texts and also two local Indo-European languages: Tocharian, spoken in the oases of Kucha and Turfan, and Khotanese, an Iranian language of the kingdom of Khotan. To write these languages the scribes created new letters for sounds absent from Sanskrit, an early example of the adaptability of the Brāhmī system.

docs.title: 12.7.2 Siddham in East Asia
docs.text: The Siddhamātṛkā script, which flourished in northern India from about the 6th to the 10th century, was carried to China with Buddhist texts and used there to write Sanskrit mantras and dhāraṇīs. The Japanese monk Kūkai (774–835), founder of the Shingon school, brought the study of Siddham (Japanese shittan) to Japan, where it is still practised as a sacred calligraphy. The ordering of the Japanese kana syllabary (the gojūon, “fifty sounds”) is generally believed to reflect the phonetic order of Sanskrit learned through these studies.

docs.title: 12.8 Writing Materials and Epigraphy
docs.text: Palm leaf The main writing material of South India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and widely used in the north. In the south the letters were incised with a stylus and the leaf rubbed with lamp-black; incision favours rounded letter forms, since straight horizontal strokes would split the leaf along its grain (Figure 12.4). Birch bark Used in Kashmir and the north-west; the Gāndhārī Buddhist scrolls and the Bakhshali mathematical manuscript are written on it. Stone and copper Inscriptions on rock, pillars, cave walls and temple walls, and land grants on copper plates, are the main sources for the history of the scripts. Tens of thousands of inscriptions are known, the majority from South India (Salomon 1998). Figure 12.5 shows a Brāhmī inscription in a cave at Kanheri. Cloth, wood and paper Paper came into use in India from about the 11th–13th centuries, spreading from the north-west and becoming common under the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals. Figure 12.4. A palm leaf from a Sanskrit manuscript of a Sāmavedic text in Malayalam script, from a collection in Thrissur, Kerala, showing the incised, rounded letter forms typical of South Indian palm-leaf writing Photo: Ms Sarah Welch, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons Figure 12.5. An inscription in Brāhmī script at Kanheri, carved on a pillar in a Buddhist rock-cut cave beside a figure of the Buddha Photo: Ms Sarah Welch, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 12.9 Dating Inscriptions
docs.text:
The development of letter forms allows an experienced epigraphist to date an undated inscription, often to within a century or two, by comparison with dated ones. Dated inscriptions use a variety of eras, whose starting points had to be worked out by modern scholars from inscriptions that mention datable events or astronomical details (Salomon 1998). The most important are listed in Table 12.4.

Table 12.4. Some eras used in Indian inscriptions Era Year 0 or 1 corresponds to Notes Vikrama 57–56 BCE Used widely in northern and western India; still in use Śaka 78 CE Used widely in western and southern India and in Southeast Asia; the basis of the Indian national calendar Gupta 319–320 CE Used in the Gupta empire and later in Gujarat (as the Valabhī era) Kalacuri–Cedi 248–249 CE Used in central and western India Harṣa 606 CE Used in northern India and Nepal Kollam 824–825 CE Used in Kerala Hijrī 622 CE Islamic lunar era, used in Persian and Arabic inscriptions

Regnal years, counted from a king’s accession, are also very common, especially in early inscriptions such as those of Aśoka, which are dated by years since his consecration.

docs.title: 12.10 Print and Digital Encoding
docs.text:
Printing in Indian scripts began with missionaries. Tamil books were printed in the 16th century by Portuguese Jesuits; a Tamil Christian catechism printed in 1578 is usually cited as the first book in an Indian script. Printing in Bengali and Devanāgarī developed in the late 18th and early 19th centuries in and around Calcutta. Charles Wilkins and the Bengali craftsman Pañcānan Karmakār cut the Bengali types for N. B. Halhed’s Bengali grammar (1778), and Pañcānan later worked for the Serampore Mission Press, which printed books in many Indian languages. The need to cast types for hundreds of conjunct consonants shaped the appearance of printed scripts, and typewriters and later computer fonts imposed further simplifications.

In the digital age, the abugida principle had to be represented in a form computers could process. The Indian standard ISCII (1991) and the international Unicode standard encode each Brāhmī-derived script as a sequence of consonant, vowel and virāma characters, arranged in the traditional phonetic order; the conjunct forms and the placement of vowel signs are then produced by the font and the rendering software. The design follows, in effect, the analysis of the phoneticians: the stored text records the sounds in their spoken order, while the visual arrangement on the page is a matter of display. Unicode now also encodes historical scripts such as Brāhmī, Kharoṣṭhī, Grantha and Śāradā, and newer ones such as Ol Chiki and Warang Citi, which makes the digital edition of inscriptions and manuscripts possible.

docs.title: 12.11 Numerals and Zero
docs.text: Brāhmī inscriptions already use special signs for numbers, but in a non-positional system with separate signs for the units, the tens, a hundred and a thousand. The decimal place-value system with nine digits and a sign for zero developed in India during the first half of the 1st millennium CE. Brahmagupta’s Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628 CE) gives rules for calculating with zero as a number. The earliest securely dated inscriptions using a zero in place-value notation are from Southeast Asia (Cambodia and Sumatra, 683–684 CE), and the earliest in India proper is an inscription at Gwalior dated 876 CE; earlier copper-plate dates in decimal notation exist but some of them are suspect. The system passed through Arabic and Persian scholarship to Europe, where its numerals are still called “Arabic”, though Arab authors called them “Indian” (Plofker 2009). Its history is treated in Volume 11, Gaṇita.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Persian, Hindavi and Urdu: The Indo-Persian Sciences of Language
docs.text:
rekhte ke tumhīṃ ustād nahīṃ ho ghālib kahte haiṃ agle zamāne meṃ koī mīr bhī thā You are not the only master of Rekhta, Ghālib; they say that in an earlier age there was also one Mīr.

— Ghālib, Urdu dīvān, ghazal 36, verse 11

docs.title: 13.1 Introduction
docs.text:
For some six centuries India had a second learned culture of language beside the Sanskrit one. Persian came to northern India with the Ghaznavids and the Delhi Sultanate. From the 13th century it was a language of government, poetry, history and scholarship, and under the Mughals it was the language of administration across most of the subcontinent until the East India Company replaced it in the courts in 1837. Persian learning carried with it a set of language sciences inherited from Arabic scholarship: morphology (ṣarf) and syntax (naḥw), lexicography (lughat), prosody (ʿarūḍ), and rhetoric in its three branches of maʿānī, bayān and badīʿ. Indian scholars worked in all of them, and in one, Persian lexicography, most of the major works of the 16th to 19th centuries were compiled in India (Alam 2003).

This tradition belongs in a history of Śabda Vidyā for three reasons. It produced a large and sophisticated literature on language that surveys centred on Sanskrit usually omit. It met the Indian languages directly: Persian scholars wrote grammars of Braj and Hindavi, compiled glossaries of Indian words, and reflected on the resemblances between Persian and the languages of India. And it shaped the emergence of Hindavi, Rekhta and Urdu, the language whose 19th-century division into Hindi and Urdu is followed in Chapter 14. The literature of Urdu is treated in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā, and the wider meeting of Islamic and Indian learning in Volume 24, Samanvaya. This chapter is concerned with the scholarship of language.

docs.title: 13.2 Arabic Grammar in Indian Learning
docs.text:
In the madrasas of Muslim India, Arabic grammar held a place comparable to that of Pāṇini in Sanskrit learning. It was the gateway to every higher subject, because the Qurʾān, ḥadīth, law and theology were studied in Arabic. The curriculum that took shape in the 18th century at Farangī Maḥall in Lucknow, known as the Dars-i Niẓāmī, became the model for much of South Asia. It began with short primers of morphology and syntax, many of them written in Persian, such as the Mīzān and the Naḥw-i Mīr. It then led students through the classic Arabic grammar of Ibn al-Ḥājib, the Kāfiya, with the Persian scholar Jāmī’s commentary on it. As in the Sanskrit schools, texts were memorised first and explained afterwards, and mastery was tested by disputation.

Indian-born scholars also made major contributions to Arabic lexicography itself. Raḍī al-Dīn al-Ṣaghānī (1181–1252), born in Lahore, compiled large Arabic dictionaries in Baghdad. Muḥammad Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (1732–1791), born at Bilgram in Awadh, settled in Cairo, where he wrote the Tāj al-ʿArūs, a vast commentary on Fīrūzābādī’s dictionary and the largest of all classical Arabic lexicons. His near-contemporary from the same town, Ghulām ʿAlī Āzād Bilgrāmī (1704–1786), wrote in Arabic as well as Persian; his Subḥat al-Marjān introduced Arabic readers to Indian figures of speech and the Indian classification of heroines (nāyikābheda) and compared them with Arabic rhetoric, a rare case of Sanskrit poetics passing into Arabic.

docs.title: 13.3.1 Why India?
docs.text: Persian lexicography flourished in India rather than in Iran for a simple reason. In Iran Persian was the mother tongue of most of its writers, who had less need of dictionaries. In India it was a learned language, acquired at school by Indian Muslims and by Hindus of the scribal and administrative classes (Kāyasthas, Khatrīs and others) who staffed the Mughal administration. These learners needed guidance on rare words, correct spelling and pronunciation, and the meanings of the words used by the classical poets. Indian lexicographers, many of them themselves second-language users of Persian, supplied it. Their position resembles that of the Sanskrit grammarians, who also described a language learned from books and teachers rather than from the household (Section 1.6).

docs.title: 13.3.2 From the Sultanate to the Mughals
docs.text: The earliest Persian dictionaries compiled in India date from the Delhi Sultanate. The Farhang-i Qawwās of Fakhr al-Dīn Mubārakshāh Qawwās, compiled in the reign of ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī (r. 1296–1316), arranged its words by subject, much as the Sanskrit kośas did (Chapter 4). In the 15th century the Sharafnāma of Ibrāhīm Qawwām Fārūqī, compiled in Bengal, glossed some of its Persian words in Hindavi. It is thus an early, if small, source for the vocabulary of the north Indian vernacular. A series of further dictionaries followed in the 15th and 16th centuries, each correcting and enlarging its predecessors, until the Mughal age produced the works that made India the centre of Persian lexicography.

docs.title: 13.3.3 The great dictionaries
docs.text:
The Farhang-i Jahāngīrī was begun on Akbar’s orders by Jamāl al-Dīn Ḥusayn Injū, a Shirazi nobleman at the Mughal court, and completed in 1608 for Jahāngīr. It opens with an extended introduction on the letters, orthography and grammar of Persian, so that it is a grammar as well as a dictionary, and it supports its definitions with citations from the poets. Its scale and authority made it the model for its successors.

The Burhān-i Qāṭiʿ, compiled at Hyderabad in 1651–52 by Muḥammad Ḥusayn Tabrīzī and dedicated to the Quṭb Shāhī sultan ʿAbd Allāh, owed its success above all to its arrangement. Earlier Persian dictionaries often followed the Arabic practice of grouping words by their final letter. The Burhān was arranged strictly by the order of the initial letters, which made it far easier to consult. It was also generous: it took in rare and archaic words, Zoroastrian terms, and a number of words drawn from the Dasātīr, a 17th-century work whose “ancient Persian” vocabulary was largely invented. These inclusions were later criticised severely. In 1861–62 the poet Ghālib, who prided himself on knowing Persian as the Iranians did, published a sharp attack on the dictionary (Qāṭiʿ-i Burhān), and a pamphlet war followed. Nevertheless the Burhān was printed at Calcutta in 1818 and translated into Ottoman Turkish. Together with the Jahāngīrī and the Rashīdī, it became a principal source of the European dictionaries of Persian compiled in the 19th century. Much of the Persian lexicon known to modern scholarship was thus first collected and sifted in India.

The Farhang-i Rashīdī (1653–54) of ʿAbd al-Rashīd of Thatta in Sindh marks a turn towards critical lexicography. Its author checked the entries of the Jahāngīrī and of the Farhang-i Surūrī, a dictionary compiled in Iran, against the usage of the poets. He rejected readings that he judged to be errors of copying, and he was sceptical of etymologies that rested on resemblance alone. The tradition continued into the colonial period with compact school dictionaries such as the Ghiyāth al-Lughāt of Ghiyāth al-Dīn Rāmpūrī (1826), which was reprinted many times.

docs.title: 13.3.4 Usage, idiom and the Hindu lexicographers
docs.text: In the 18th century the emphasis shifted from rare words to idiom and usage (muḥāvara), especially the usage of the poets of the “fresh style” (tāza-gūʾī) of the 16th and 17th centuries, many of whom wrote in India. The leading works of this kind were by Hindu scholars. Lālā Tek Chand “Bahār” of Delhi, who moved in Ārzū’s circle, compiled the Bahār-i ʿAjam (1739–40), a large dictionary of Persian idioms and phrases, each illustrated by verses from the poets. Ānand Rām “Mukhliṣ”, a Khatrī official and poet, compiled a dictionary of idioms and current usage, the Mirʾāt al-Iṣṭilāḥ (mid-1740s). That some of the most authoritative Persian lexicographers of the age were Hindus is a reminder that Persian learning in India was not confined to Muslims. It was the shared professional culture of the Mughal service elite. The Bahār-i ʿAjam remains one of the richest sources for the meaning of Persian idioms.

docs.title: 13.4 Ārzū and the Agreement of Languages
docs.text:
Sirāj al-Dīn ʿAlī Khān Ārzū (1687/88–1756) was the most important Persian philologist of 18th-century India. Born in the region of Gwalior and Agra, he spent most of his career in Delhi and died in Lucknow. He was a poet, a critic, the compiler of a large biographical anthology of Persian poets (Majmaʿ al-Nafāʾis) and a teacher of poets in both Persian and Rekhta. He was also a relative and early patron of the Urdu poet Mīr Taqī Mīr. His philological works include the Sirāj al-Lughat, a critical companion to the older dictionaries; the Chirāgh-i Hidāyat, on the idioms of the later poets; the Navādir al-Alfāẓ, a corrected and enlarged edition of an earlier Hindavi–Persian glossary (Section 13.6); and the Muthmir (“Fruitful”), a treatise on the Persian language itself (Dudney 2022).

In the Muthmir Ārzū discussed what he called tavāfuq al-lisānayn, the “agreement of the two languages”. He meant the many words that Persian and the Indian vernacular (Hindī) have in common. The phenomenon is easy to illustrate: Persian mādar and Hindi mātā “mother”, Persian nām and Hindi nām “name”. Ārzū distinguished such agreement from mere borrowing in either direction, and he treated it as a matter for serious philological attention rather than coincidence. Ārzū did not propose a family tree or a common ancestral language, and his framework was not that of 19th-century comparative philology. His observations can nonetheless be compared, as a modern analogy, with the recognition a generation later that the Iranian and Indic languages are closely related (Chapter 14). There is no evidence that William Jones, whose address of 1786 drew on Persian learning, knew of the Muthmir (Dudney 2022).

Ārzū was equally modern in his view of linguistic authority. He held that languages change with time and place, and that a usage established among competent Indian writers of Persian was correct even if it differed from the speech of Iran. The view was put to the test after the Iranian poet Shaykh ʿAlī Ḥazīn settled in India in the 1730s. Ḥazīn mocked the Persian of Indian poets as faulty, and Ārzū answered him in a critique of Ḥazīn’s own verse, the Tanbīh al-Ghāfilīn (“Warning to the Heedless”). The controversy was a debate about who owns a cosmopolitan language: its native speakers, or the wider community that writes it. It has an interesting parallel in the Sanskrit grammarians’ appeal to the usage of the cultivated (śiṣṭa), not the speech of any one region, as the standard of correctness (Chapter 7). In the next century Ghālib’s attack on the Burhān reopened the question from the opposite side, in favour of Iranian authority.

docs.title: 13.5 Sanskrit and Persian
docs.text:
Learning also ran between Persian and Sanskrit. Under the Mughals many Sanskrit works were translated into Persian, among them the epics and, in 1657, the Upaniṣads by Dārā Shukōh; this history is followed in Volume 24, Samanvaya. In the other direction, a small number of Sanskrit works taught Persian to readers of Sanskrit. Audrey Truschke has traced a series of Sanskrit lexicons and grammars of Persian from the 14th to the 17th century (Truschke 2012). Two examples stand out. The Pārasīprakāśa of Kṛṣṇadāsa, composed at Akbar’s court, is a grammar of Persian in Sanskrit with a glossary, which describes Persian nouns and verbs in the categories of Sanskrit grammar, with cases as vibhakti and tenses as lakāra. A second work of the same name, by Vedāṅgarāya (1643), was written for Shāh Jahān as a glossary of the Persian and Arabic terms of astronomy and astrology. These works are the mirror image of the Persian grammars of Indian languages. Each tradition described the other in its own categories, as the Pāli and Tamil grammarians had earlier used the categories of Sanskrit (Chapters 9 and 10).

The best-known Persian account of an Indian language is Mīrzā Khān’s Tuḥfat al-Hind (“Gift from India”), written around 1675 for a Mughal prince. It is an encyclopaedia of the learning a cultivated reader needed to enjoy Hindi (Braj) poetry. It explains the Indian script and how Indian sounds, such as the retroflex and aspirated consonants, can be written in Persian letters; it gives a grammar of Braj; it treats prosody (piṅgal), rhetoric (alaṅkār), the theory of rasa and music (the last discussed in Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya); and it ends with a glossary of Hindi words (Busch 2011). It is the first systematic grammar of Braj. It is not the first description of a modern Indo-Aryan language: Dāmodara’s Uktivyaktiprakaraṇa had explained an Old Kosali vernacular in the 12th century in the course of teaching Sanskrit, and Thomas Stephens’s grammar of Konkani had been printed in 1640 (Section 9.11). But it is among the first to treat a vernacular as a literary language with a grammar of its own. Its treatment of Braj prosody and poetics shows how much of the Sanskrit sciences of language reached Persian readers through the vernacular literatures.

docs.title: 13.6.1 The names of a language
docs.text: The language that became modern Hindi and Urdu had many names before it had a standard form, and the names themselves record its history (Faruqi 2001; Rahman 2011). Hindavī or Hindī (“of Hind”) was the usual name in Persian sources from the Sultanate onwards for the vernacular of north India, as opposed to Persian. In the Deccan sultanates the same language, carried south by soldiers, officials and Sufis, developed a literature of its own from the 15th century and was called Dakanī (Dakhni); in Gujarat a related literary idiom was called Gujrī. Rekhta (“poured, mixed”) was at first the name of a style of poetry that mixed Persian and Hindavi; in the 18th century, when Delhi poets took up the ghazal in the vernacular, it became the name of the literary language itself, and Mīr and later Ghālib called their Urdu verse Rekhta. Urdu comes from the phrase zabān-i urdū-yi muʿallā, “the language of the exalted camp (or court)”, meaning Shāhjahānābād (Delhi), and is not attested as the name of the language before the last decades of the 18th century. Hindustani was the name preferred by many European writers for the common spoken language of the north.

docs.title: 13.6.2 Glossaries and the Persian view of Hindavi
docs.text: Persian scholars first approached Hindavi through glossaries. A popular genre of rhymed vocabularies for schoolchildren, modelled on the Arabic–Persian Niṣāb al-Ṣibyān, produced Persian–Hindavi versions. The best known is the Khāliq Bārī, traditionally attributed to Amīr Khusrau (1253–1325), though most scholars consider it a later work. In the late 17th century ʿAbd al-Wāsiʿ Hānsawī compiled the Gharāʾib al-Lughāt, a glossary of Hindavi words with their Persian equivalents. Ārzū’s corrected version of it, the Navādir al-Alfāẓ, adds critical comments on pronunciation and usage. Together they are among the most valuable records of the vocabulary of north Indian speech before the 19th century. Walter Hakala has shown how these works helped define what counted as a language and as a correct word in the multilingual world of Mughal India (Hakala 2016).

docs.title: 13.6.3 European grammars and Gilchrist
docs.text: European interest in Hindustani began with the trading companies. The Dutch East India Company’s agent Joan Josua Ketelaar wrote a grammar of Hindustani in Dutch around 1698, of which a Latin version was printed at Leiden in 1743; the Halle missionary Benjamin Schultze published a Grammatica Hindostanica in 1745; and the British officer George Hadley published grammatical remarks on the “vulgar dialect of the Indostan language” in 1772. The decisive figure was John Borthwick Gilchrist (1759–1841), a Scottish surgeon. His Dictionary, English and Hindoostanee (1787–90) and Grammar of the Hindoostanee Language (1796) made him the leading European authority, and in 1800 he became the first head of the Hindustani department of the College of Fort William in Calcutta. Gilchrist distinguished several registers of the language: a Persianised “High Court” style, a “Middle” or genuine Hindustani style that he recommended to British officers, and a “Hinduwee” style closer to rural speech and Sanskrit. He insisted on a Roman transcription of his own design. The prose texts he commissioned from his Indian staff at Fort William, in what came to be called Urdu and Hindi, and the institutional consequences of separating them, are discussed in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 13.6.4 Inshā’s Daryā-yi Laṭāfat
docs.text: The first comprehensive description of Urdu by Indian authors was written, characteristically, in Persian. The Daryā-yi Laṭāfat (“Sea of Elegance”, 1807–08) is by the poet Inshā Allāh Khān “Inshā” (1752–1817) of Lucknow, with a second part by his colleague Mirzā Muḥammad Ḥasan Qatīl on prosody and rhetoric. It covers the sounds and grammar of Urdu. More unusually, it describes the varieties of the language as spoken by different groups: the people of the various quarters of Delhi, the speech of women, and the usage of Hindus and Muslims, Punjabis and easterners. Inshā’s standard of eloquence (faṣāḥat) was the speech of the cultivated Delhi elite, and he judged other varieties against it. The standard tied linguistic correctness to social rank, and the book’s portraits of other people’s speech are often condescending. As a record of linguistic variation around 1800, however, it has no parallel. Inshā was also a virtuoso of registers. In his Rānī Ketakī kī Kahānī he set himself to write a story with no Persian or Arabic words at all. It is an early sign of the consciousness of vocabulary that was later to separate Hindi from Urdu.

docs.title: 13.7 Assessment
docs.text: The Indo-Persian sciences of language were scholarship by and for second-language users of a cosmopolitan language. That is why they were so strong in lexicography and usage, and why questions of authority, of who decides what is correct, were so central to them. In this they resemble the Sanskrit tradition more than is usually recognised. They also connect that tradition with the modern period. The Persian dictionaries of India became sources of European Persian scholarship. Ārzū’s reflections on the agreement of Persian and Hindi show that the resemblances between Iranian and Indian words were a subject of philological attention in India a generation before Jones’s address, though within a framework of their own that did not include a common ancestor. And the Persian descriptions of Braj, Hindavi and Urdu, from Mīrzā Khān to Inshā, are among the earliest grammars of the north Indian vernaculars; the oldest of them precede the European grammars of Hindustani that are usually treated as the beginning of their study.

  • Dudney, Arthur. 2022. India in the Persian World of Letters: Khān-i Ārzū Among the Eighteenth-Century Philologists. Oxford University Press.. — On Ārzū, his dictionaries and his philology.
